questions.title: Profiles vs. Permission Sets
questions.prompt: What's the actual difference between a profile and a permission set in Salesforce, and why can't you just do everything with profiles alone?
questions.modelAnswer: A profile is the single, mandatory baseline every user must have exactly one of -- it sets object permissions, field-level security, apps, tabs, page layout assignment, and system permissions as a floor of access. A permission set is additive and optional -- a user can have zero, one, or many of them, and each one grants additional object, field, or system permissions on top of whatever the profile already allows. The practical reason you can't rely on profiles alone is that profiles encourage building a large number of near-duplicate profiles (one per tiny access variation), which becomes a maintenance nightmare; permission sets let you keep a small number of broad, role-based profiles and layer specific extra capabilities (like access to a new custom object, or an export permission) onto only the users who need them, without cloning a profile for one extra checkbox.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain it with the mental model I actually use day to day: profile answers 'who is this user, fundamentally' -- sales rep, support agent, admin -- and sets the floor. Permission sets answer 'what extra things does this specific person or group of people need on top of that floor.' If I only used profiles, every time one sales rep needed access to a new object the rest of the sales team didn't need yet, I'd be stuck either cloning the whole Sales Rep profile into a near-duplicate just for that one difference, or giving everyone that access whether they needed it or not. With permission sets, I keep one clean Sales Rep profile and just assign the one extra permission set to the people who actually need it. Salesforce has also pushed hard toward this pattern -- Permission Set Groups let me bundle several permission sets together and assign the bundle in one step, which is usually cleaner than maintaining permissions through profile cloning at all.

Not mentioning that a user has exactly one profile but can have many permission sets
Missing the real-world consequence: profile-only management leads to profile sprawl/cloning
Forgetting permission sets can also grant app and system permissions, not just object/field access
keyPoints: A profile is mandatory, singular, and sets the baseline; permission sets are optional, multiple, and additive
Permission sets never take access away -- they only add to what the profile allows
Profile-only management tends to create profile sprawl through cloning
Permission Set Groups bundle multiple permission sets for easier assignment

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes mandatory/singular profile from optional/multiple permission sets
Explains that permission sets are additive only, never restrictive

questions.title: Permission Set Groups
questions.prompt: What problem do Permission Set Groups solve that individual permission sets don't, and what's a 'muting permission set' used for inside one?
questions.modelAnswer: A permission set group bundles multiple individual permission sets into a single unit you assign to a user in one action, instead of assigning each permission set separately and having to remember the full list every time someone joins a role. The problem it solves is assignment overhead and consistency: if a 'Senior Support Agent' role actually needs six different permission sets, assigning the group once guarantees every person in that role gets the same combination, rather than relying on an admin to remember and manually re-apply six individual assignments. A muting permission set is the mechanism for the one case a plain bundle can't handle on its own: when the group as a whole should NOT grant one specific permission that one of its component permission sets includes -- the muting permission set subtracts that specific permission back out of the group's combined effective access, without editing the original permission set (which might still be used elsewhere, unmuted).
questions.professionalAnswer: In practice I reach for permission set groups the moment I notice I'm assigning the same three or four permission sets to the same group of people repeatedly -- at that point it's clearly a role-level bundle, not a one-off, and bundling it removes the risk that I forget one of the four the next time someone joins that role. The muting permission set is the part people usually haven't run into yet: say one of the permission sets in my bundle grants 'Modify All Data' as a side effect because it was built for a different use case, but I don't want that specific group to have it. Instead of forking a whole new permission set just to remove one permission, I add a muting permission set inside the group that explicitly mutes just that one permission. The original permission set stays intact for wherever else it's used; only this group's effective access is reduced.

Not knowing muting permission sets exist, or assuming you'd have to edit/fork the original permission set instead
Thinking muting removes access the profile grants (it only mutes permissions from permission sets inside the group)
Missing the consistency/maintenance benefit as the core reason to use groups
keyPoints: Permission set groups bundle multiple permission sets into one assignable unit
The core benefit is consistent, low-effort assignment for a role that needs several permission sets
A muting permission set subtracts one specific permission back out of a group's combined access
Muting doesn't touch the original permission set, which may still be used unmuted elsewhere

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what a permission set group bundles and why
Identifies the consistency/maintenance benefit over manual assignment

questions.title: Organization-Wide Defaults
questions.prompt: What does an Organization-Wide Default (OWD) setting actually control, and why is 'Private' usually the safer starting point even though it means you'll need more sharing rules later?
questions.modelAnswer: Organization-Wide Defaults set the baseline, most-restrictive level of record access every user gets to records they don't own, for a given object, before any role hierarchy, sharing rule, or manual share widens it. OWD never grants more access than it specifies at the baseline level -- it's a floor that other mechanisms (role hierarchy, sharing rules, teams, Apex sharing) can only add to, not override downward for records already covered. 'Private' is usually the safer starting point because record-level security is much easier to reason about and audit when you widen access deliberately, one explicit sharing rule at a time, than when you start from Public Read/Write and have to explain, retroactively, why a specific group of users shouldn't see certain records -- going from open to restricted after the fact means finding and fixing every place that over-broad default was already being relied on.
questions.professionalAnswer: Whenever I'm setting up record access for a new object, I treat OWD as the one decision that's expensive to get wrong later, so I default to Private and build up from there with sharing rules, role hierarchy, and teams -- rather than starting at Public Read/Write because it's less work up front. The reasoning is really about direction of change: tightening access later means I have to find every workflow and every report that was silently depending on broad visibility and might break when I restrict it, and I usually don't find all of them before someone complains. Loosening access later with an explicit sharing rule is much safer, because I'm adding a clearly scoped exception on top of a restrictive baseline, and I can see exactly who it affects before I activate it. So yes, starting at Private means writing more sharing rules over time, but each one is a deliberate, auditable decision instead of an assumption baked into the org from day one.

Thinking OWD can be overridden downward by a sharing rule (it can only be widened, never restricted, by those mechanisms)
Choosing Public Read/Write by default 'to keep things simple' without weighing the later cost
Confusing OWD (object-level default) with field-level security (attribute-level) or CRUD (profile-level)

Role hierarchy, sharing rules, teams, and Apex sharing can only grant more access than OWD, never less

Tightening access later is much harder than loosening it later with a scoped sharing rule

questions.title: The Role Hierarchy's Effect on Record Access
questions.prompt: How does the role hierarchy affect record visibility, and what's the difference between what it does for a standard object versus a custom object with 'Grant Access Using Hierarchies' unchecked?
questions.modelAnswer: The role hierarchy automatically grants users in a higher role the same record-level access their subordinates have, for records owned by or shared with those subordinates -- a regional manager can see what their reps see without a separate sharing rule, because visibility rolls up the hierarchy by default. For standard objects, this rollup behavior is built in and can't be turned off: the hierarchy always grants that upward access. For a custom object, Salesforce exposes 'Grant Access Using Hierarchies' as an explicit checkbox on the OWD setting, and if it's unchecked, the role hierarchy's automatic upward grant is turned off for that object specifically -- managers don't automatically see their subordinates' custom-object records just because they're above them in the hierarchy; access has to come from an explicit sharing rule or other mechanism instead.
questions.professionalAnswer: The way I think about it: on standard objects like Opportunity or Case, the role hierarchy's upward visibility is just always on, by design, and you can't disable it from the OWD screen. On a custom object, Salesforce actually gives you the choice, because not every custom object's data should automatically roll up the management chain -- maybe it's something sensitive where a manager shouldn't automatically see every record just because they outrank the owner. If I uncheck 'Grant Access Using Hierarchies' on a custom object's OWD, I'm explicitly saying the hierarchy doesn't apply here, and anyone who needs cross-level visibility into that object has to get it through an actual sharing rule instead of inheriting it for free by being a manager. It's a subtle setting that trips people up in interviews because they assume hierarchy behavior is uniform across every object, when custom objects are actually the one place it's configurable.

Not knowing 'Grant Access Using Hierarchies' is a custom-object-only, OWD-level checkbox
Thinking unchecking the box removes a manager's existing access rather than stopping the automatic future grant
Confusing role hierarchy rollup with manual sharing or sharing rules, which are separate mechanisms

questions.title: What Sharing Rules Can and Can't Do
questions.prompt: What exactly does a sharing rule do, and why can't a sharing rule ever be used to restrict access below what the OWD already grants?
questions.modelAnswer: A sharing rule automatically grants a defined group of users additional access to records owned by, or meeting criteria matched by, another defined group -- for example, 'everyone in the Support role gets Read access to Opportunities owned by anyone in the Sales role,' or a criteria-based rule like 'all Cases with Priority = High are shared Read/Write with the Escalations queue.' A sharing rule structurally can't restrict access below OWD because sharing rules are, by design, additive-only mechanisms layered on top of the OWD baseline -- Salesforce's record-access model only ever widens visibility as you move from OWD to role hierarchy to sharing rules to manual shares, never narrows it, so there is no sharing-rule setting that removes access OWD already granted; if OWD is Public Read/Write, no sharing rule can make a subset of users unable to read a record.
questions.professionalAnswer: The way this comes up practically: if someone asks me to 'write a sharing rule so this one group can't see these records,' I have to explain that's not something a sharing rule can do -- if those records are visible to that group because of an overly broad OWD setting, the actual fix is tightening the OWD (and then using sharing rules to re-open access for whoever genuinely needs it), not trying to carve out an exception downward. Sharing rules come in two flavors I use constantly: owner-based (grant access based on who owns the record, usually role- or group-based) and criteria-based (grant access based on field values on the record itself, regardless of owner). Both only add access on top of OWD and role hierarchy -- they're a one-way lever. That's actually a feature, not a limitation, because it means I can always reason about a record's maximum possible visibility just by knowing OWD, and sharing rules only ever make a user's access a superset of that floor, never a subset.

Not distinguishing owner-based sharing rules from criteria-based sharing rules

Missing that the fix for 'too much access from a sharing rule' standpoint is usually to tighten OWD, not add a restrictive rule

Owner-based and criteria-based are the two sharing rule types
To reduce over-broad access, the fix is a tighter OWD, not a restrictive sharing rule (which doesn't exist)

questions.title: Field-Level Security vs. Page Layouts
questions.prompt: A field is marked 'Visible' on a page layout but the user still can't see it on the record. Walk through why field-level security and page layouts are two separate, both-required permissions, and which one actually takes precedence.
questions.modelAnswer: Page layouts and field-level security (FLS) answer two different questions, and both have to say yes before a field shows up for a given user: the page layout controls where a field appears and whether it's shown on that particular layout at all, while FLS (set on the profile or granted via a permission set) controls whether that user is allowed to see or edit that field's data at all, on any layout, in any context including list views, reports, and APIs. FLS is the one that takes precedence in the sense that it's the actual security control -- a field can be placed prominently on a layout, but if FLS marks it 'Field Hidden' for the user's profile (and no permission set grants visibility), the field will not render for that user anywhere, including that layout, because FLS is enforced platform-wide, not just on page layouts.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is a classic 'it's on the layout, why can't they see it' support ticket, and the first thing I check is always FLS, not the layout, because the layout is a UI arrangement decision while FLS is the actual access control. I think of it like a window and a lock: the page layout is the window -- it determines where the field would be visible if you could see through it at all -- but FLS is the lock on the window; if it's locked (Field Hidden), it doesn't matter how prominently the window is placed, nothing shows through it. So my troubleshooting order is: check the user's profile's field-level security for that field first; if it's set to Visible there, check whether a permission set is overriding it to Hidden (permission sets can't hide a field the profile exposes, only grant more -- so if it's still invisible, the profile itself is the culprit); only after confirming FLS allows it visible do I even look at whether the layout itself includes the field at all.

Assuming FLS and page layout are redundant/interchangeable settings
Not knowing permission sets can only grant FLS access, never hide a field the profile already shows
Troubleshooting the layout first instead of checking FLS first, which is the actual access gate

FLS is the real security control; the page layout is purely a UI arrangement
Permission sets can grant additional FLS visibility but can never hide a field the profile exposes
The correct troubleshooting order is FLS first, then the layout

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains that both FLS and layout placement are required

questions.title: Data Loader vs. the Import Wizard
questions.prompt: When would you reach for the Import Wizard instead of Data Loader, and what's the actual technical reason Data Loader can do things the Import Wizard can't?
questions.modelAnswer: The Import Wizard is the right tool for small, simple, guided loads -- a few thousand records or fewer, on a handful of supported standard objects (plus any custom object) with its own point-and-click duplicate-matching step built in, run from inside the browser with no install. Data Loader is the right tool once you need scale, automation, or object flexibility the wizard doesn't offer: it supports every object including ones the wizard doesn't, handles millions of records in batches, can run from the command line on a schedule, and critically supports hard delete and true upsert using an external ID key across relationships, none of which the Import Wizard exposes. The underlying technical reason is that Data Loader talks directly to the Bulk API (or SOAP API for smaller jobs), giving it low-level control over batch size, operation type, and field mapping, while the Import Wizard is a simplified, opinionated UI layered on top of a narrower set of those same underlying capabilities, deliberately trading flexibility for ease of use.
questions.professionalAnswer: My rule of thumb: if it's a one-time, few-thousand-record cleanup on a standard or simple custom object and the built-in duplicate matching is good enough, I use the Import Wizard because it's faster to set up and safer for someone less comfortable with CSV mapping. The moment I need any of a few specific things, I switch to Data Loader -- upserting against an external ID (especially when I'm loading related records and need to resolve relationships by external ID instead of Salesforce ID), loading an object the wizard doesn't support, doing a true hard delete instead of send-to-recycle-bin, or needing to script the load so it can run unattended. Technically, Data Loader is just a more direct client over the Bulk/SOAP APIs, so it exposes operations the API supports that the wizard's UI simply never built a screen for -- it's not that Data Loader has secret extra power, it's that it doesn't hide any of the API's real capability behind a simplified wizard flow.

questions.title: External IDs and Upsert Operations
questions.prompt: What is an External ID field for, and why does using one for an upsert operation matter so much when you're loading related records from an outside system?
questions.modelAnswer: An External ID field is a custom field (text, number, or email type) marked as an external ID, which lets Salesforce index it for fast lookups and -- critically -- use it as the matching key for an upsert operation, instead of requiring you to already know the record's internal Salesforce ID. Upsert means 'update if a record matching the key already exists, insert if it doesn't,' and the reason this matters enormously for related records from an outside system is that the external system's own identifiers (a legacy customer number, an ERP order ID) are the only IDs you actually have in your source file -- Data Loader can match parent-child relationships during a load by external ID (using a special relationship field reference) without you first having to run a lookup pass to translate every external identifier into a Salesforce ID before the load.
questions.professionalAnswer: Where this becomes essential rather than just convenient is multi-object loads with relationships -- say I'm loading Contacts that need to link to Accounts, and my source system only gives me each account's legacy ERP number, not its Salesforce ID. If Accounts already have an External ID field populated with that ERP number, I can load Contacts with a relationship reference like Account.MyExternalId__c equal to the ERP number straight from the source file, and Data Loader resolves that to the correct Account's Salesforce ID automatically during the insert. Without that external ID field, I'd have to do a separate extract of every Account's Salesforce ID, build a cross-reference table, and manually re-map every Contact row to the right Salesforce ID before I could load anything -- external ID turns a multi-step manual mapping exercise into a single load Data Loader handles for me, and it also makes future re-loads from the same source idempotent, since upserting by the same external ID just updates the existing record instead of creating a duplicate.

Not explaining upsert's insert-or-update behavior clearly
Missing the relationship-resolution benefit when loading related records across objects
Not mentioning idempotency -- that re-running the same load by external ID won't create duplicates

questions.title: Matching Rules vs. Duplicate Rules
questions.prompt: What's the difference between a matching rule and a duplicate rule in Salesforce's duplicate management, and can you have one without the other?
questions.modelAnswer: A matching rule defines HOW two records are compared to decide if they're likely the same real-world entity -- which fields to compare (name, email, phone), and which matching method to use per field (exact, fuzzy, acronym, and so on). A duplicate rule defines WHAT HAPPENS when a matching rule finds a likely duplicate -- which record types/objects the check runs on (on create, on edit, or both), whether the action is to block the save, allow it with a warning, or just report it, and which specific matching rule(s) to use for that comparison. You can't have a functioning duplicate rule without a matching rule, because the duplicate rule's job is entirely about the response to a match, not the matching logic itself -- it always points to one or more matching rules to do the actual comparison; you can, however, have a matching rule defined and active without any duplicate rule referencing it, in which case it's available for manual duplicate-check actions (like the 'Find Duplicates' action on a record) but won't automatically trigger anything on save.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd frame it as 'the matching rule is the brain, the duplicate rule is the behavior' -- the matching rule decides what counts as a likely match (do I treat two accounts with the same name but different addresses as duplicates, or require both to match), and the duplicate rule decides what Salesforce does once it finds one. In practice I almost always build the matching rule first, test it against real data to make sure it's not too loose (flagging unrelated records) or too strict (missing real duplicates), and only then wire a duplicate rule to it with the action I actually want -- usually 'Alert' with a warning on create for leads, since blocking outright can frustrate reps dealing with a legitimately different person who happens to share a common name. Salesforce does ship standard matching rules for Account, Contact, and Lead out of the box, which is why some orgs appear to have duplicate management working without anyone having built a custom matching rule -- they're just using the standard one.

Thinking a duplicate rule can exist and function with no matching rule behind it

Missing that the duplicate rule's action (block/warn/report) is configurable, not fixed

questions.title: Tabular, Summary, Matrix, and Joined Reports
questions.prompt: Walk through the four Salesforce report formats -- tabular, summary, matrix, and joined -- and explain what each one is actually for, not just what it looks like.
questions.modelAnswer: Tabular is a flat row-and-column list with no grouping -- good for a simple list you'll export or feed into another tool, but it can't be used as a dashboard source for a chart because it has no groupings to chart against. Summary adds one or more groupings (rows) with subtotals, which is the workhorse format for most business reporting -- 'Opportunities grouped by Stage, subtotaled by Amount.' Matrix groups by both rows AND columns simultaneously, producing a true grid -- useful when you need to see a value at the intersection of two independent dimensions, like Sales Rep down the side and Month across the top, which a summary report (grouping only by rows) can't represent as cleanly. Joined reports let you combine multiple report types (effectively multiple distinct data sets) into one report with separate blocks that can share common groupings, which is what you reach for when you need Opportunities and Cases, say, side by side filtered by the same account, and neither a summary nor a matrix report can mix two unrelated report types in one view.
questions.professionalAnswer: When I'm picking a format, I ask what the actual question is first. If it's just 'give me the raw list,' tabular, and I accept it can't drive a dashboard component. If it's 'show me totals by one dimension' -- Opportunities by Stage, Cases by Priority -- that's summary, and it's genuinely the one I use most often because most business questions really do reduce to one grouping with subtotals. If the question has two independent dimensions at once -- rep by month, product by region -- I reach for matrix, because trying to force that into a summary report means awkward nested groupings that don't actually answer 'what's the number for this rep in this month' as directly as a grid does. Joined reports are the one I use least, but they're the right tool specifically when a stakeholder wants two genuinely different objects' data next to each other on one page filtered the same way -- I've used it for an account-health view blending Opportunities and open Cases for the same set of accounts, which no single report type could pull alone.

questions.title: Dashboard Components and Filters
questions.prompt: What's the difference between a dashboard filter and the underlying report's own filters, and why would you add a filter at the dashboard level instead of just filtering the source report?
questions.modelAnswer: A report's own filters are baked into that specific report and apply every time it runs, regardless of who's viewing a dashboard built from it. A dashboard filter sits on top of the dashboard itself, lets the person viewing the dashboard interactively narrow what every filterable component shows (for example, by Region or Owner) without editing any underlying report, and the filter only affects that viewing session -- it doesn't change the source reports for anyone else. The reason to add a filter at the dashboard level rather than the report level is exactly that interactivity: a report-level filter is fixed for everyone who runs that report, while a dashboard filter lets one dashboard serve many different viewers who each want to slice the same set of components differently -- a VP looking at the whole company and a regional manager looking at just their region can use the same dashboard and just apply a different dashboard filter value, instead of needing a separate report (and dashboard) built per region.
questions.professionalAnswer: I think of report filters as the fixed lens the data is captured through, and dashboard filters as a way to let the viewer adjust the view afterward without touching that lens. If I hard-code 'Region = East' into the underlying report's filter, every component built from that report is permanently scoped to East, for every viewer, which means I'd need to duplicate the whole dashboard per region if different people need different regions. Instead, I leave the report broader, add a dashboard filter on Region, and now the same single dashboard works for anyone -- they just pick their region from the filter and every applicable component updates for that view only. There is a real limit worth knowing: not every component is filterable this way, and dashboard filters only work on fields present in the underlying reports, so if I want to filter on a field a given component's report doesn't actually have, that component just won't respond to the dashboard filter at all.

Not mentioning that dashboard filters only work on fields present in the underlying report(s)

questions.title: Lookup vs. Master-Detail Relationships
questions.prompt: What actually changes in Salesforce's behavior when you choose Master-Detail instead of Lookup for a relationship field, beyond 'one is required and one isn't'?
questions.modelAnswer: Master-detail creates a tight ownership relationship: the detail record's security (sharing, visibility) is controlled entirely by the master -- the detail has no OWD, sharing rules, or role hierarchy setting of its own; it inherits the master's. Deleting the master record cascades and deletes every detail record automatically (there's no orphaning). Roll-up summary fields are only possible on the master, summarizing its details, and this is the main reason people pick master-detail at all. The detail's master-detail field is required and cannot be left blank, and in a standard master-detail you can't reparent a detail record to a different master without special configuration. Lookup, by contrast, is a loose reference: the related record has its own independent sharing settings, deleting the parent does not delete the child (the lookup field just becomes blank unless you've set a specific delete-behavior restriction), no roll-up summary is possible, and the field can be optional and reparentable by default.
questions.professionalAnswer: The question I actually ask before choosing is 'does this child record's existence and visibility genuinely depend on its parent, to the point that it makes no sense without one?' If yes -- like Opportunity Line Items, which don't mean anything detached from an Opportunity -- master-detail fits, and I get roll-up summaries almost for free, like a total line-item amount rolling up to the Opportunity. If the relationship is more of a loose association -- a Case referencing an Account, where the Case still makes sense (and should still be visible under its own security) even if that reference changes or the Account doesn't control who can see the Case -- lookup is correct, and I'd never use master-detail there, because I don't want deleting an Account to cascade-delete every related Case. The cascading delete behavior alone is the thing that bites people who pick master-detail casually for the roll-up summary feature without registering that it also means the parent now controls the child's fate, not just its summary.
commonMistakes: Only mentioning required vs. optional, missing cascading delete and inherited security
Not knowing roll-up summary fields require master-detail
Thinking lookup relationships can also cascade-delete by default
Missing the ownership/security inheritance distinction as the core conceptual difference
keyPoints: Master-detail: detail inherits master's security, cascading delete, roll-up summaries possible, required field
Lookup: independent security, no cascading delete, no roll-up summary, optional and reparentable by default
The real decision test is whether the child record's existence/visibility genuinely depends on the parent
Roll-up summary fields are the main reason people pick master-detail, but cascading delete is the real tradeoff

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains security inheritance difference
Correctly explains cascading delete behavior
Correctly ties roll-up summary availability to master-detail
Gives a realistic decision test/example

questions.title: Record Types and Page Layout Assignment
questions.prompt: What does a record type actually control, and why do you still need a separate page layout assignment step even after creating one?
questions.modelAnswer: A record type controls which subset of picklist values are available on a record (for example, limiting Lead Status to a different set of values for a 'Partner Lead' record type than a 'Direct Lead' one) and, for objects that support it, which business process (sales process, support process, lead process) applies. On its own, a record type does NOT determine which page layout a user sees -- that's a genuinely separate configuration: the page layout assignment matrix, which maps a combination of profile and record type to a specific page layout. You need that separate step because the same record type might reasonably need a different layout for different profiles (a 'Partner Lead' might show extra fields to the Partner Relations team's profile that a general Sales profile doesn't need to see), so Salesforce deliberately decouples 'what values and process apply' (record type) from 'what the screen looks like for this profile' (layout assignment).
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain it as two different questions that happen to both start with creating a record type: first, 'what values and process should apply when someone picks this record type' -- that's the record type definition itself, including which picklist values are active for it. Second, and separately, 'what should the screen actually look like for each profile that can use this record type' -- that's the page layout assignment matrix, found on the record type's detail page or the object's Page Layouts settings, where you explicitly map Profile x Record Type to a Page Layout. The mistake I see constantly is someone creates a shiny new record type, assumes it'll 'just work,' and then every profile defaults to whatever layout was already assigned (often the master layout) because nobody went into the assignment matrix and pointed the new record type, for the relevant profiles, at the actual layout meant for it. Both steps are mandatory and neither one implies the other.
commonMistakes: Thinking a record type automatically determines or changes the page layout
Not knowing the assignment is a profile x record type matrix, not a single global setting
Describing record types as only a picklist-value feature, missing the business process angle
Assuming creating a record type is sufficient without a separate assignment step
keyPoints: A record type controls available picklist values and the applicable business process
Page layout assignment is a separate step mapping profile x record type to a specific layout
The two are decoupled deliberately, since the same record type can need different layouts per profile
Forgetting the assignment step is the most common reason a new record type 'doesn't work'

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what a record type controls
Correctly explains that layout assignment is separate
Describes the profile x record type assignment matrix accurately
Mentions the common real-world mistake of skipping assignment

questions.title: Building a Permission Set Group for a New Role
questions.prompt: A new 'Senior Support Agent' role needs three existing permission sets (Case Escalation, Knowledge Management, Refund Approval) but should NOT have the 'Modify All Data' permission that happens to be bundled inside the Refund Approval permission set. Walk through exactly how you'd set this up.
questions.modelAnswer: First, go to Setup > Permission Set Groups > New, name it something like 'Senior Support Agent,' and add the three existing permission sets (Case Escalation, Knowledge Management, Refund Approval) to its list of included permission sets -- the group's combined access is the union of all three. Next, since 'Modify All Data' from Refund Approval shouldn't apply to this group, create a new Muting Permission Set scoped to this group, and inside it, explicitly mute the 'Modify All Data' system permission. Add that muting permission set to the group. Finally, assign the completed Permission Set Group to the Senior Support Agent users; verify by checking one test user's effective access (via their user detail page or a permission set assignment summary) to confirm Modify All Data is not present for them, while the other permissions from all three included sets are.
questions.professionalAnswer: Practically, I'd start by confirming in the existing Refund Approval permission set exactly which object/system permission is granting Modify All Data, so I'm muting the right thing and not guessing. Then I build the group, add all three permission sets, and before assigning it to anyone, I add the muting permission set and mute specifically that one system permission -- I don't touch the original Refund Approval permission set at all, because other roles might still need it with Modify All Data intact. After assigning the group to one test user first, I'd log in as that user (or use 'Login As') and verify directly that Modify All Data behavior is actually gone -- for example, trying an action that would only work with that permission -- rather than just trusting the setup screen, because muting interacts with multiple permission sets in a group and I want to confirm the net effect, not just the configuration intent.
commonMistakes: Editing the original Refund Approval permission set directly instead of using a muting permission set
Muting at the wrong permission (muting a different object permission instead of the system permission actually granting Modify All Data)
Skipping verification with a test user and assuming the configuration is correct
Assigning the group before adding the muting permission set, requiring rework
keyPoints: Permission set groups bundle existing permission sets without duplicating them
A muting permission set subtracts one specific permission from the group's combined access
The original permission set is left untouched, since other roles may still need it
Verify the net effect with a test user rather than trusting the setup screen alone

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly builds the permission set group with the three sets
Correctly uses a muting permission set rather than editing the source permission set
Mutes the correct permission (Modify All Data specifically)
Includes a verification step with a test user

questions.title: Assigning a New Page Layout to a Record Type
questions.prompt: You've created a new 'Partner Opportunity' record type on Opportunity and built a corresponding 'Partner Opportunity Layout' with extra fields. Right now, every profile is still seeing the old default layout for this record type. Walk through the exact steps to fix that.
questions.modelAnswer: Go to Object Manager > Opportunity > Page Layouts and confirm the Partner Opportunity Layout exists with the right fields. Then go to Object Manager > Opportunity > Record Types, open the Partner Opportunity record type, and find the 'Page Layout Assignment' related section (or use the dedicated Page Layout Assignment matrix accessible from Page Layouts). In that matrix, for each profile that should see the new layout when working with Partner Opportunity records, change the assigned layout from the current default to Partner Opportunity Layout -- the matrix is Profile (rows) x Record Type (columns), so this has to be done per relevant profile, not once globally. Save, then verify by opening an existing Partner Opportunity record (or creating a new one) logged in as a user with one of the updated profiles and confirming the new fields appear.
questions.professionalAnswer: The step people skip is realizing the assignment is per-profile, not a single global switch -- so I'd go into the assignment matrix (Setup > Object Manager > Opportunity > Page Layouts > Page Layout Assignment) and look specifically at the column for Partner Opportunity across every row (profile). For profiles where partner-facing teams actually work this record type, I'd click Edit Assignment and point them at Partner Opportunity Layout; for profiles that never touch this record type, I'd leave them alone rather than touching every row just because I'm in the screen. After saving, I always test as an actual user with one of the changed profiles rather than just trusting the matrix, because it's easy to update the wrong row/column intersection in a large matrix and not notice until someone reports the old layout is still showing.
commonMistakes: Assuming creating the record type or layout alone changes what users see
Changing every profile's assignment instead of only the profiles that need the new layout
Confusing the Profile x Record Type matrix direction and editing the wrong cell
Not verifying the change as an actual affected user afterward
keyPoints: Layout assignment is a separate, mandatory step after creating a record type and layout
The assignment matrix is Profile x Record Type -- changes are per-profile, not global
Only update the profiles that actually need the new layout for this record type
Always verify as a real user with an affected profile

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the Page Layout Assignment matrix as the fix location
Correctly describes editing per relevant profile, not globally
Describes a sensible save/verification step
Avoids unnecessary changes to unrelated profiles

questions.title: Configuring OWD Plus a Sharing Rule for a New Object
questions.prompt: You've just created a custom object, 'Vendor Contract,' and the requirement is: nobody can see another department's contracts by default, but everyone in the Legal role needs read-only access to every contract regardless of department. Walk through the configuration.
questions.modelAnswer: First, set the Vendor Contract OWD to Private (Setup > Sharing Settings > find Vendor Contract > Organization-Wide Defaults > set Default Internal Access to Private), which establishes that nobody sees another department's/owner's records by default. Then create a criteria-based or role-based sharing rule: since the requirement is 'Legal sees everything regardless of department,' a role-based sharing rule naming 'Legal' as the role to grant access TO, with the rule scoped to apply to all records (owned by anyone, often expressed as 'records owned by members of a public group containing all other roles' or simply a criteria rule with no restrictive filter matching all records), with access level set to Read Only. Save, then verify by creating test Vendor Contract records owned by different department users and confirming a Legal-role test user can see all of them read-only, while a non-Legal user in a different department cannot see another department's contract.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start at Sharing Settings and lock down Vendor Contract to Private first, since that's the baseline the rest depends on -- getting this backwards (building the sharing rule before the OWD is actually restrictive) can make it harder to tell whether the rule is doing anything, since Private isn't yet enforced. Then I'd create a new sharing rule under Vendor Contract Sharing Rules: Rule Type 'based on record owner' if ownership maps cleanly to department, selecting 'owned by members of' the departments/roles that aren't Legal (or, more simply, a criteria-based rule with essentially no filter so it matches every record), granting access TO the Legal role (and, if Legal has subordinate roles that should also see it, including those via 'Roles and subordinates'), Access Level: Read Only. After saving, I'd test with at least two users -- a Legal user confirming they see contracts from multiple departments, and a non-Legal user from Department A confirming they can't see Department B's contract -- because testing only the 'access granted' side and not the 'access still denied elsewhere' side is how these configurations slip through with gaps.
commonMistakes: Building the sharing rule before setting OWD to Private, making the rule's effect hard to verify
Confusing 'based on record owner' sharing rules with criteria-based ones when department isn't reflected by ownership
Granting Read/Write when the requirement specifically says read-only
Only testing that access was granted, not that access is still correctly denied elsewhere
keyPoints: Set OWD to Private first to establish the restrictive baseline
Choose owner-based vs. criteria-based sharing rule depending on how department maps to the data
Grant access TO the Legal role at the correct access level (Read Only per the requirement)
Test both the granted-access case and the still-denied case with different test users

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly sets OWD to Private as the first step
Correctly configures a sharing rule granting Legal read-only access
Chooses a sensible rule type (owner-based or criteria-based) with justification
Includes a two-sided verification step

questions.title: Building a Role Hierarchy for a Growing Sales Team
questions.prompt: A sales org currently has one flat 'Sales Rep' role for everyone. They've just hired two Regional Sales Managers, each managing a group of reps, and a VP of Sales above both. Walk through how you'd restructure the role hierarchy.
questions.modelAnswer: Go to Setup > Roles, and build the hierarchy top-down: create or confirm a top-level role (CEO or similar), add a 'VP of Sales' role reporting to it, then add two 'Regional Sales Manager' roles (East, West, or named by territory) reporting to VP of Sales, and finally either split the existing flat 'Sales Rep' role into two region-specific rep roles (reporting to the matching Regional Sales Manager) or, if keeping one Sales Rep role is acceptable, recognize that a single shared rep role under two different managers isn't directly expressible -- so in practice you create 'Sales Rep - East' and 'Sales Rep - West' roles, each reporting to its respective Regional Sales Manager role. Then reassign each existing user to their correct new role (via the user record's Role field), replacing the old flat role. Finally, verify: a Regional Sales Manager should automatically see their own region's reps' records (if role-hierarchy-based access applies to the relevant objects), and the VP should see both regions' data, without needing new sharing rules for that specific rollup.
questions.professionalAnswer: The part that trips people up is realizing you generally can't have one role report to two different parent roles, so if reps are genuinely split by region with a different manager each, you need two rep-level roles, not one shared one -- I'd create 'Sales Rep - East' under 'Regional Sales Manager - East' and 'Sales Rep - West' under 'Regional Sales Manager - West,' both ultimately rolling up to 'VP of Sales.' I'd build this top-down in Setup > Roles so every role has its parent already in place before I create the next level down, then go user by user and update each rep's and manager's Role field to the new structure -- this reassignment step is really the bulk of the actual work and the one most likely to get missed or rushed. Once that's done, the role hierarchy's built-in upward visibility means a Regional Sales Manager automatically sees their region's reps' Opportunities without me writing a single new sharing rule, and the VP sees everything beneath both managers -- that automatic rollup is the entire point of restructuring the hierarchy instead of just renaming one role.
commonMistakes: Trying to have a single role report to two different parent roles
Building roles bottom-up instead of top-down, creating orphaned roles temporarily
Forgetting the user reassignment step -- creating the roles but leaving users on the old role
Assuming new sharing rules are needed for manager rollup when role hierarchy already provides it automatically
keyPoints: Role hierarchies are built top-down, with each role needing its parent in place first
A single role generally can't report to two different parent roles -- split roles by region/manager instead
Reassigning existing users to new roles is a required, often-missed step
Role hierarchy provides automatic upward visibility rollup without additional sharing rules

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly designs a hierarchy without a role reporting to two parents
Describes building top-down with roles in the right order
Includes the user reassignment step explicitly
Correctly explains the automatic rollup benefit

questions.title: Setting Field-Level Security for a Sensitive Field
questions.prompt: A new custom field, 'Social Security Number (Encrypted)__c,' needs to be visible and editable only to users with the 'HR Specialist' profile, invisible to everyone else, including System Administrators who don't also hold that profile. Walk through the configuration.
questions.modelAnswer: Go to Object Manager > the relevant object > Fields & Relationships > the SSN field > Set Field-Level Security (or edit FLS from the field's detail page). For every profile EXCEPT HR Specialist -- including System Administrator -- uncheck both Visible and Read-Only (set the field to fully hidden). For the HR Specialist profile specifically, check Visible and leave Read-Only unchecked so it's editable. Save. If any users need visibility without being on the HR Specialist profile (say, an HR Director on a different profile), grant it via a targeted permission set rather than changing the field's profile-level default, since permission sets can only add visibility and this keeps the restrictive default intact for everyone else.
questions.professionalAnswer: The detail that matters here is explicitly including System Administrator in the 'hide this field' list -- it's easy to assume admins automatically bypass FLS, but they don't; 'Modify All Data' bypasses record-level sharing restrictions, not field-level security, so if I leave Visible checked on the System Administrator profile out of habit, admins who aren't HR Specialists would still see the field, which defeats the purpose. So I'd go through every profile in the FLS editor, deliberately unchecking Visible (and Read-Only) everywhere except HR Specialist, rather than assuming hiding it from 'everyone' happens automatically. If, afterward, someone outside HR Specialist genuinely needs access -- an HR Director on the general Admin profile, say -- I wouldn't change this field's profile-level setting for a broad profile just for one person; I'd build a small permission set granting Read (and Edit if needed) on that one field and assign it only to that person, keeping the restrictive baseline intact for everyone else.
commonMistakes: Assuming System Administrator automatically bypasses field-level security
Leaving FLS at default (often Visible) on profiles other than HR Specialist by oversight
Widening a broad profile's FLS instead of using a targeted permission set for exceptions
Forgetting Read-Only also needs to be considered, not just the Visible checkbox
keyPoints: FLS must be explicitly restricted per profile; it defaults open unless changed
Modify All Data bypasses sharing, not field-level security -- admins aren't automatically exempt
Every profile except HR Specialist should have the field fully hidden (not visible, not read-only)
Exceptions for individuals should go through a targeted permission set, not a broad profile change

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly configures FLS to hide the field from all profiles except HR Specialist
Correctly identifies that System Administrator is not automatically exempt
Describes using a permission set for individual exceptions
Mentions handling both Visible and Read-Only appropriately

questions.title: Upserting Related Records with Data Loader Using an External ID
questions.prompt: You need to load 5,000 new Contacts from a legacy CRM export into Salesforce, linking each Contact to its correct Account using the legacy system's Account number (not the Salesforce Account ID). Walk through the Data Loader steps.
questions.modelAnswer: First, confirm the Account object already has a custom External ID field (for example, Legacy_Account_Number__c) populated with each account's legacy number -- if it doesn't exist yet, create it and backfill it before touching Contacts. Prepare the Contact CSV with a column for the legacy account number. In Data Loader, choose Upsert as the operation (not Insert, since some contacts may already exist from a prior partial load) on the Contact object, select the Legacy_Account_Number__c-based relationship field when mapping -- specifically mapping the CSV's legacy number column to Account.Legacy_Account_Number__c, which Data Loader resolves to the correct Account automatically -- and map the remaining Contact fields normally. Run the load against a sandbox first with a small sample, check the success/error log, confirm Contacts landed under the correct Accounts, then run the full load against production.
questions.professionalAnswer: The step I wouldn't skip is validating the Account side first -- if even a handful of Accounts are missing their Legacy_Account_Number__c value, every Contact meant to link to one of those will fail the relationship resolution, so I'd run a quick report or export on Account to confirm the external ID field is fully populated before touching Contacts at all. In Data Loader, I'd pick Upsert rather than plain Insert specifically because this kind of legacy migration often gets re-run or has overlapping batches, and Upsert makes reruns safe; for Contacts themselves, if there's also a legacy contact ID I want to upsert against, I'd use that as the Contact's own key, while separately mapping the Account relationship through Legacy_Account_Number__c in the field mapping screen. I always run a 20-50 row test batch in a sandbox first and actually open a few resulting Contact records to confirm they're attached to the right Account, not just that the load reported success, because a wrong-but-successful relationship mapping is the kind of error that doesn't show up as a failure in the log.
commonMistakes: Running Insert instead of Upsert when records may already exist from a prior partial load
Not validating the Account's external ID field is fully populated before loading Contacts
Mapping the legacy number to a plain text field on Contact instead of the Account relationship reference
Skipping a small sandbox test batch before the full production load
keyPoints: Validate the parent object's external ID field is populated before loading related child records
Upsert is the safer operation for migrations likely to be re-run or run in batches
The CSV's legacy identifier maps to the relationship field (Account.ExternalId), not a plain text field
Test with a small batch in a sandbox and verify actual relationships, not just load success

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly validates/prepares the Account external ID field first
Correctly chooses Upsert and explains why
Correctly describes mapping the relationship via the external ID field
Includes a sandbox test-batch verification step

questions.title: Using the Import Wizard's Duplicate Matching
questions.prompt: You're importing 800 new Leads from a trade show list using the Import Wizard, and you want to avoid creating duplicate Leads for people already in the system. Walk through how the Import Wizard's matching step actually works and what you'd do with the results.
questions.modelAnswer: Launch the Import Wizard (Setup > Data Import Wizard), choose Leads as the object, and select Add new records (or Add new and update existing, depending on whether some trade show contacts might already be Leads). On the matching step, the wizard shows which field(s) it'll use to detect duplicates against existing records -- typically Email for Leads -- and lets you choose how to handle matches it finds: for new-record-only imports, matched rows are typically skipped and reported rather than created as duplicates. After mapping the remaining CSV columns to Lead fields and running the import, review the results summary, which separates successfully created records from skipped/matched ones, and check the skipped list to confirm those were genuine existing Leads rather than false matches on a shared field like a generic company email address.
questions.professionalAnswer: Before I even open the wizard, I'd skim the trade show CSV for obvious issues -- a lot of attendees share a company's general inquiries@ email address instead of a personal one, and if the wizard is matching Leads on Email, that generic shared address could cause legitimate separate people to get skipped as 'duplicates' of each other or of an existing Lead that also used that address. Assuming the data's reasonably clean, I'd run the import choosing to add new records, let the wizard's built-in duplicate check run against Email, and then actually open the results report afterward rather than just checking it completed -- specifically reviewing anything flagged as skipped to confirm those really were the same person and not a false match, since 800 records is few enough to spot-check the skipped list by hand. If I find false positives caused by a shared email pattern, I'd rather fix the matching assumption (or clean that column) and re-run than just accept the wizard's default outcome blindly.
commonMistakes: Not reviewing the skipped/matched results, assuming the wizard's duplicate detection is always correct
Not anticipating a shared/generic email field causing false-positive duplicate matches
Choosing 'Add new records' when some trade show leads may already exist as Leads needing an update instead
Treating the import as done once it runs, without spot-checking actual outcomes
keyPoints: The Import Wizard's duplicate check typically matches on a key field like Email for Leads
Matched records are skipped (or updated, depending on the chosen action) rather than duplicated
Shared or generic email addresses in source data can cause false-positive matches
Always review the results report, especially the skipped/matched list, rather than trusting it blindly

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes the wizard's matching mechanism and options
Anticipates a realistic data-quality risk (shared emails) affecting matching
Describes reviewing results rather than trusting the run blindly
Chooses an appropriate action (new vs. new-and-update) with reasoning

questions.title: Setting Up a Duplicate Rule for Accounts
questions.prompt: Sales ops wants new Accounts with a matching company name AND matching billing state to be blocked from being created, but an exact name match alone (different state) should just show a warning, not block. Walk through setting this up.
questions.modelAnswer: This needs a matching rule that compares on both Account Name (exact or a reasonably strict fuzzy match) and Billing State (exact), so first build or confirm a custom matching rule combining those two field comparisons with AND logic -- note the standard out-of-the-box Account matching rule typically only matches on Name, so a custom matching rule is likely needed here rather than the default one. Then create a duplicate rule on Account referencing that custom matching rule, with the action set to Block on create (and optionally on edit), since the requirement calls for a hard block when both conditions match. For the softer 'name matches but state differs' case, since that's a different matching condition, either build a second matching rule (Name only) paired with a second duplicate rule set to Alert (warn, don't block), or rely on the standard Name-only matching rule already in the org for that warning-level rule, keeping the two duplicate rules and their matching rules clearly separated by what they check and what they do.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd build this as two separate matching-rule-and-duplicate-rule pairs rather than trying to cram both behaviors into one rule, because a single duplicate rule has one action (block or alert), not a conditional 'block if X, warn if Y.' Pair one: a matching rule checking Name exact AND Billing State exact, wired to a duplicate rule with action Block -- this is the hard stop sales ops wants. Pair two: a matching rule checking Name alone (which might just be the standard Account matching rule already available), wired to a separate duplicate rule with action Alert -- this is the softer warning. I'd test both carefully with real-ish data: create a test Account, then try creating a near-duplicate with the same name and same state (expecting a block), and a second near-duplicate with the same name but a different state (expecting a warning, not a block) -- confirming both rules fire independently and don't conflict with each other is the actual proof the setup is correct, not just that each rule saved without an error.
commonMistakes: Trying to express both behaviors (block vs. warn) in a single duplicate rule, which only supports one action
Using the standard Name-only matching rule for the block case when the requirement specifically needs Name AND State
Not testing both scenarios (same name+state vs. same name only) to confirm the rules don't conflict
Forgetting duplicate rules need to be marked active to actually take effect
keyPoints: A duplicate rule has exactly one action; different behaviors need separate rule pairs
The block case needs a custom matching rule combining Name AND Billing State
The warn case can likely reuse a simpler Name-only matching rule
Test both scenarios explicitly to confirm the two rules behave independently and correctly

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly recognizes two separate matching/duplicate rule pairs are needed
Correctly configures the block case (Name AND State, action Block)
Correctly configures the warn case (Name only, action Alert)
Includes a concrete testing plan for both scenarios
