questions.title: Building a Matrix Report of Sales by Rep and Month
questions.prompt: Sales leadership wants to see total closed-won Opportunity amount broken down by Sales Rep (rows) and Close Month (columns), in a single grid. Walk through building this report.
questions.modelAnswer: Create a new report, choose the Opportunities report type, and set the format to Matrix. Add a filter for Stage equals Closed Won (and set the date range filter on Close Date to the relevant period). Add a row grouping on Opportunity Owner (the Sales Rep) and a column grouping on Close Date, grouped by Month. Drag Amount into the Sum summarize-by field so each cell shows the summed closed-won amount for that rep/month intersection, with row and column grand totals appearing automatically. Save the report, and optionally save it to a shared folder sales leadership can access, then preview it to confirm the grid actually reads correctly -- reps down the side, months across the top, dollar totals in the cells.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start from the Opportunities report type specifically, not a generic one, since Close Date and Stage are standard Opportunity fields I need for the filters. After switching the format to Matrix (this is a dropdown at the top of the report builder, easy to miss if you're used to building summary reports), I'd add the Closed Won stage filter and a sensible date range first, before worrying about groupings, so I'm not looking at a huge, slow preview of every historical Opportunity while I'm still configuring it. Then I'd drag Opportunity Owner into the row grouping area and Close Date (grouped by Month, which is a grouping-level setting I'd explicitly set rather than leaving at the default) into the column grouping area, and finally make sure Amount is set to Sum in the summarize panel -- by default a new numeric field sometimes defaults to Average, which would silently give leadership the wrong number if I didn't check it.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to switch the format from Summary to Matrix explicitly
Leaving Amount summarized by Average instead of Sum, giving a misleading total
Not grouping Close Date specifically by Month, leaving it ungrouped or grouped by day
Building without a Stage and date-range filter first, making the report slow and cluttered while configuring
keyPoints: Matrix format groups by both rows (Rep) and columns (Month) simultaneously
Explicitly set the summarize-by field to Sum, not the possible default of Average
Group the date field by Month at the column-grouping level
Add filters (Stage, date range) early to keep the report manageable while building

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly selects Opportunities report type and Matrix format
Correctly sets row grouping (Owner) and column grouping (Close Month)
Correctly sets Sum (not Average) on Amount
Includes appropriate filters (Stage, date range)

questions.title: Adding a Region Filter to an Existing Dashboard
questions.prompt: An existing sales dashboard has five components all built from reports that include a Region field, but currently every viewer sees all regions at once. Walk through adding a single dashboard filter so viewers can narrow to their own region.
questions.modelAnswer: Open the dashboard in Edit mode, and use the Add Filter option (usually near the top of the dashboard builder). Choose Region as the filter field -- the field picker will only show fields that exist on the underlying reports of at least one component, so if Region doesn't appear as an option, that's a sign at least one report doesn't actually expose that field for filtering. Confirm which components the filter will apply to (components built from reports without Region simply won't respond to it); if all five are built from reports containing Region, they should all pick it up automatically. Save the dashboard, then test by applying a specific region value and confirming all five components update to reflect only that region, and that grand totals/numbers visibly change rather than just the chart's appearance.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd open the dashboard builder and look for Add Filter first, and before committing to Region as the field, I'd actually check each of the five components' source reports to confirm Region is a field present in all of them -- because the Add Filter field picker will only let me choose fields available on at least one component, which means it's possible to add a Region filter that silently does nothing for one or two components if their underlying report doesn't have that field at all. Assuming all five do have it, I'd select Region, save, and then actually test it as the final step by picking a specific region value and checking that every component's numbers genuinely change, not just that the filter control appeared on the page -- a filter that renders but doesn't actually affect every intended component is a real failure mode I've seen, usually traced back to one report using a slightly different field name for region than the others.
commonMistakes: Assuming the filter will automatically apply to all components without checking each report has the field
Not testing by applying an actual value and confirming numbers change, just checking the filter control appears
Confusing a dashboard filter with editing each underlying report's own filter individually
Not noticing a differently-named region field on one report causing that one component to not respond
keyPoints: Dashboard filters only work on fields present in the underlying report(s) of each component
Verify every component intended to respond to the filter actually has the field in its source report
Test with an actual filter value applied, confirming real number changes, not just UI appearance
A component built from a report missing the filter field simply won't respond to it

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes adding the dashboard filter via the builder
Correctly checks that underlying reports expose the filter field
Includes a genuine verification step applying a real value
Identifies a realistic failure mode (field name mismatch)

questions.title: Creating a Master-Detail Relationship Field
questions.prompt: You're building a custom 'Warranty Claim' object that should always belong to exactly one 'Service Order' custom object record, should be deleted automatically if the Service Order is deleted, and needs a roll-up count of claims per order. Walk through creating the relationship field.
questions.modelAnswer: On the Warranty Claim object, go to Fields & Relationships > New, choose Master-Detail Relationship as the field type, and select Service Order as the related (master) object. Name the field appropriately (for example, Service_Order__c), and note that Salesforce will prompt about sharing settings -- since Warranty Claim is the detail, it inherits Service Order's sharing automatically, so there's no separate OWD to set for Warranty Claim on this relationship. Complete the field creation wizard (field-level security, page layout placement). Once the master-detail field exists, go to the Service Order object, add a new Roll-Up Summary field, choose Warranty Claim as the object being summarized, set the summary type to COUNT, and optionally add a filter if only certain claims should count. Save and test by creating a Service Order, adding a couple of Warranty Claims under it, and confirming the roll-up count updates, then deleting the Service Order and confirming its Warranty Claims are deleted too.
questions.professionalAnswer: The field type choice is the first and most important decision -- Master-Detail Relationship, not Lookup, because I need both the cascading delete behavior and the roll-up summary capability, and roll-up summaries simply aren't available across a lookup. When I create the field, Salesforce will walk me through sharing settings for the detail object, which I'd note but not worry about configuring separately, since Warranty Claim as the detail just inherits whatever sharing Service Order has. After the relationship field exists, I'd go build the roll-up on Service Order itself (roll-ups always live on the master, summarizing the detail, never the other way around) -- Count of Warranty Claims, no filter unless there's a reason to exclude some claims (like excluded/voided ones). Before calling it done, I'd actually test the cascading delete specifically, since that's the behavior most likely to surprise someone later if it's wrong -- deleting a test Service Order and confirming its Warranty Claims go with it, not get orphaned.
commonMistakes: Choosing Lookup instead of Master-Detail, which would prevent the roll-up summary and cascading delete requirements
Trying to put the roll-up summary field on the detail object instead of the master
Not testing the cascading delete behavior explicitly before considering the setup complete
Forgetting that the detail object's sharing settings become dependent on the master once master-detail is created
keyPoints: Master-Detail is required here for both cascading delete and roll-up summary capability
Roll-up summary fields are created on the master object, summarizing the detail
The detail object inherits the master's sharing settings automatically
Test cascading delete explicitly, since it's the behavior most likely to be assumed rather than verified

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly chooses Master-Detail over Lookup with justification
Correctly places the roll-up summary field on the master object
Correctly configures the roll-up as COUNT
Includes explicit testing of cascading delete

questions.title: Creating a Roll-Up Summary Field for Total Line Item Amount
questions.prompt: On a standard Opportunity-to-Opportunity Line Item relationship (already master-detail), sales ops wants a field on Opportunity showing the sum of all line items' discounted total, excluding any line item marked 'Voided.' Walk through building this.
questions.modelAnswer: On the Opportunity object, go to Fields & Relationships > New, choose Roll-Up Summary as the field type, name it something like Total_Line_Item_Amount__c, and select the summarized object as Opportunity Line Items (or the custom object acting as line items, if this isn't the standard Product/Price Book line item relationship). Choose SUM as the summary type and select the field representing discounted total on the line item (for example, Total_Price__c). In the filter criteria section, add a condition: Voided equals False (or Voided not equal to True, matching however that checkbox/picklist is structured), so voided line items are excluded from the sum. Save, then test by creating an Opportunity with several line items, marking one as Voided, and confirming the roll-up total correctly excludes it.
questions.professionalAnswer: Roll-up summary fields only work across a master-detail relationship, so the first thing I'd confirm is that the Opportunity-to-Line-Item relationship in this org is genuinely master-detail (it is, for the standard Opportunity Product relationship) -- if this were a custom lookup-based 'line item-like' object instead, I'd have to explain that a roll-up isn't possible there at all without converting the relationship. Assuming it is master-detail, I'd create the roll-up with SUM on whatever field holds the already-discounted line total, and the part I wouldn't skip is the filter criteria -- without a 'Voided = False' filter, every voided line item would still count toward the total, silently overstating Opportunity value. I'd test this specifically by creating a line item, voiding it, and confirming the roll-up number drops back to exclude it, rather than just confirming the roll-up computes a number at all, since a roll-up that sums everything including voided items would look correct at a glance while being wrong.
commonMistakes: Attempting a roll-up summary across a lookup relationship, which isn't supported
Choosing SUM on the wrong field (e.g., list price instead of the discounted total)
Forgetting the filter criteria to exclude Voided line items, silently overstating totals
Testing only that a number appears, not that voided items are actually excluded from it
keyPoints: Roll-up summary fields require a master-detail relationship -- not possible over a lookup
Select the correct underlying field (discounted total, not list price) for the SUM
Filter criteria within the roll-up excludes records that shouldn't count (Voided = False)
Test explicitly that excluded/voided records don't affect the computed total

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly confirms master-detail is required and in place
Correctly configures SUM on the right field
Correctly adds filter criteria excluding Voided line items
Includes a specific test confirming exclusion works

questions.title: A Profile Change Broke Access for One Team
questions.prompt: After you tightened the Sales Rep profile's object permissions to remove an unused 'Delete' permission on Opportunities, the Sales Operations team -- who are also on the Sales Rep profile -- suddenly can't clean up duplicate test Opportunities anymore. How do you diagnose and fix this without just reverting the whole change?
questions.modelAnswer: The root issue is that Sales Ops shares the same profile as regular reps, so a permission change meant for the broader rep population affected a subgroup that actually needed that permission for a legitimate reason -- this is itself a sign the profile was doing too much work for too varied a group. Rather than reverting the change (which brings back Delete for everyone, including the reps who shouldn't have it), the fix is to create a small permission set granting Delete on Opportunity, and assign it specifically to the Sales Ops users -- restoring exactly the access they need without restoring it for the whole Sales Rep population. Going forward, this is also a signal to consider whether Sales Ops should be split onto its own profile if the divergence in what they need grows beyond this one permission.
questions.professionalAnswer: First thing I'd confirm is actually why it broke -- checking that Delete is indeed what's missing (rather than, say, a sharing/OWD issue that happens to coincide with the timing) by looking at the exact error Sales Ops gets when they try to delete. Once I confirm it's the removed object permission, I wouldn't just revert my change, because the original problem (reps having an unused delete permission they shouldn't) is still real for the rest of the team -- reverting throws that fix away to solve one subgroup's need. Instead, I'd build a narrow permission set, something like 'Opportunity Cleanup - Delete,' granting just Delete on Opportunity, and assign it only to the Sales Ops users who actually do this cleanup work. That restores their specific capability surgically. I'd also make a note that if Sales Ops keeps needing exceptions like this, it might be worth giving them their own profile down the line instead of continuing to patch exceptions onto the shared Sales Rep profile one permission set at a time.
commonMistakes: Reverting the entire profile change instead of fixing the specific affected group
Not confirming the actual cause (assuming it's the permission change without checking the real error)
Granting the permission back at the profile level, undoing the original security improvement entirely
Not considering whether the affected group needs its own profile if this keeps happening
keyPoints: Diagnose the actual cause before assuming which change caused it
Fix narrowly with a permission set rather than reverting for everyone
A shared profile across groups with different real needs is itself a sign of a structural issue
Consider a longer-term fix (separate profile) if exceptions keep recurring

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses rather than assumes the cause
Avoids reverting the broader security improvement
Proposes a permission set as the surgical fix
Notes the structural profile-sharing issue for the future

questions.title: A Field Is on the Layout but Still Invisible to a User
questions.prompt: A user reports that a 'Discount Approved' checkbox field, which you can clearly see on their assigned page layout in Setup, simply isn't showing up on their record view. What's your troubleshooting sequence?
questions.modelAnswer: The layout showing the field in Setup only proves the layout's definition includes it -- it doesn't prove the field will render for a specific user, because field-level security (FLS) is a separate, and ultimately the real, gatekeeper. The sequence: first check the user's profile's FLS setting for Discount Approved -- if it's set to Field Hidden there, that alone explains it regardless of the layout. Second, check whether any permission set assigned to the user affects this field -- remembering permission sets can only grant visibility, not hide it, so if the profile already shows it but the user still can't see it, a permission set isn't the cause. Third, confirm the user is actually assigned the page layout you're looking at (check their profile and record type combination against the assignment matrix) -- it's possible they're seeing a different layout than the one you inspected. Only after FLS and the correct-layout-assignment are both confirmed would I suspect something else, like a Lightning page component-level visibility rule hiding that specific field.
questions.professionalAnswer: My instinct here is immediately to not trust that 'I can see it in the layout editor' means anything about what this specific user sees, because that's purely the layout's field list -- it says nothing about FLS. So step one, I go to the field's Set Field-Level Security screen and check this specific user's profile row; if it's hidden there, that's almost certainly the whole answer, and no layout change will fix it. If FLS looks fine on the profile, step two is double-checking I'm actually looking at the right layout for this user -- I'd check their profile and the record's record type against the Page Layout Assignment matrix, because it's entirely possible there are two similar layouts and this user is actually on a different one than the one I happened to open. If both of those check out, I'd consider something more specific to Lightning -- a component or field visibility rule on the Lightning record page itself, which is a layer beyond the classic page layout and FLS that can still hide a field conditionally.
commonMistakes: Assuming the layout being correct in Setup means the field will show for every user on it
Not checking FLS first, when it's usually the actual cause
Not verifying the user is even on the layout being inspected (checking the assignment matrix)
Stopping the investigation at the layout level without considering Lightning page-level visibility rules
keyPoints: A field visible on a layout in Setup doesn't guarantee a specific user sees it -- FLS is the real gate
Check the user's actual profile's FLS setting for the field first
Confirm the user is actually assigned that specific layout via the assignment matrix
Consider Lightning page component-level visibility rules if FLS and layout both check out

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies FLS as the primary suspect, not the layout itself
Describes checking the correct layout assignment for this specific user
Correctly reasons about permission sets' additive-only nature
Considers a further layer (Lightning page visibility) if basics check out

questions.title: A User Sees Far Fewer Records Than Expected
questions.prompt: A newly promoted Regional Sales Manager reports they can only see their own Opportunities, not their team's, even though the OWD for Opportunity is Private and the role hierarchy should grant them visibility into their reports' records. Where do you look?
questions.modelAnswer: First, verify the manager's user record actually has the correct Role assigned -- the single most common cause of 'role hierarchy isn't working' is that the user simply isn't in the role you think they're in, or their reports aren't actually beneath their role in the hierarchy tree. Second, confirm the reps' User records have their Role field pointing to a role that is genuinely a child of the manager's role -- it's easy to have roles that look hierarchically related by name but aren't actually nested correctly in Setup > Roles. Third, double-check this is a standard object (where hierarchy rollup can't be disabled) versus a custom object, where 'Grant Access Using Hierarchies' might be unchecked on the OWD, explicitly turning off the rollup for that object. Fourth, rule out a more specific override -- a restriction rule or a sharing recalculation that hasn't run yet after a recent role change, since sharing rules based on roles can take time to recalculate after a hierarchy change.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start with the most boring, most common cause: open the manager's user record and the reps' user records and actually look at the Role field values, rather than assuming the org chart in someone's head matches what's configured. I've seen this exact issue be nothing more than the manager being freshly promoted and their user record still showing the old role, or the reps never having been moved under the new manager's role at all. If roles genuinely look correct, I'd check the actual hierarchy tree in Setup > Roles to confirm the rep roles are nested under the manager's role, not just named similarly while sitting elsewhere in the tree. If this is a custom object rather than standard Opportunity, I'd also check 'Grant Access Using Hierarchies' on the OWD, since that's the one place hierarchy rollup can be deliberately turned off. And if a role was just restructured, I'd consider that sharing recalculation can lag slightly after a hierarchy change, so I'd check back after confirming a recalc has completed before assuming the fix didn't work.
commonMistakes: Assuming the role hierarchy itself is broken before checking the actual Role field values on user records
Not verifying the reps' roles are truly nested under the manager's role in the hierarchy tree
Forgetting 'Grant Access Using Hierarchies' can be unchecked on custom object OWD
Not accounting for sharing recalculation lag after a recent role change
keyPoints: Check user records' actual Role field assignments first -- the most common real cause
Confirm roles are genuinely nested correctly in the hierarchy tree, not just similarly named
For custom objects, check whether 'Grant Access Using Hierarchies' is unchecked
Recent role changes may need sharing recalculation time before access reflects correctly

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Starts troubleshooting with the simplest, most likely cause (role assignment)
Checks the hierarchy tree structure itself, not just role names
Considers the custom-object hierarchy-grant checkbox
Mentions sharing recalculation timing

lessonLink.label: Review: Roles and the Role Hierarchy

questions.title: A Sharing Rule Isn't Granting the Expected Access
questions.prompt: You created a criteria-based sharing rule granting Read access to Cases where Priority equals 'Critical,' shared with the Escalations public group. Testing shows users in that group still can't see critical Cases owned by other people. What do you check?
questions.modelAnswer: First, confirm the rule is actually Active -- sharing rules can be saved but not activated, and an inactive rule has zero effect even though it looks fully configured. Second, verify the test users are actually members of the Escalations public group the rule references -- group membership changes don't always get noticed, and nested groups (a group containing another group) can be a source of confusion about who's really a member. Third, double-check the criteria itself matches real data exactly -- if Priority is a picklist, confirm the rule's criteria value matches the exact API value/label Salesforce expects (a rule built against 'Critical' when the actual value is 'Critical ' with trailing whitespace from a bad import, or a different case, won't match). Fourth, remember sharing rule changes can take time to recalculate across existing records -- a rule created after the Case records already existed may need a manual sharing recalculation (Setup > Sharing Settings > Recalculate) to apply retroactively to already-existing Cases, since it otherwise may only apply going forward for new/edited records in some scenarios.
questions.professionalAnswer: My troubleshooting order: active status first, because it's the single fastest thing to check and the most common oversight -- a rule sitting there configured but not activated behaves exactly like it doesn't exist. Then I'd check that my test user is actually in the Escalations public group, by opening the group and looking at its member list directly rather than trusting that I added them correctly earlier. If both of those are fine, I'd go look at an actual Critical Case record and compare its Priority value precisely against what the rule's criteria specifies -- picklist value mismatches (trailing spaces, a slightly different label from the API value) are a classic silent failure. Finally, if the rule and group and criteria all look right but older Cases still aren't shared, I'd run a manual sharing recalculation from Setup, since sharing rules don't always retroactively apply to records that existed before the rule was created without that explicit recalculation step.
commonMistakes: Not checking whether the sharing rule is actually Active
Assuming group membership is correct without checking the group's actual member list
Not considering a picklist value mismatch (whitespace, label vs. API name) in the criteria
Not knowing sharing recalculation may be needed for the rule to apply to pre-existing records
keyPoints: Confirm the sharing rule is Active, not just saved
Verify actual public group membership directly, not from memory
Check for exact criteria value matches, including whitespace/label vs. API name issues
Run a manual sharing recalculation if the rule needs to apply retroactively to existing records

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Checks rule activation status first
Verifies actual group membership
Considers criteria value mismatch as a cause
Mentions sharing recalculation for pre-existing records

questions.title: Data Loader Upsert Fails on Every Row with an External ID Error
questions.prompt: You run a Data Loader upsert job mapping Contact rows to Accounts via an External ID field, and every single row fails with an error about the external ID field not being found or not unique. What are you checking first?
questions.modelAnswer: If every row fails identically, the problem is almost certainly structural, not data-specific, so first confirm the field you're mapping to on Account is actually marked as an External ID (and, for true upsert matching, also marked Unique) in its field definition -- a text field that merely has similar-sounding data but was never checked as External ID/Unique in Setup can't be used as an upsert key and will throw exactly this kind of error. Second, confirm the exact API name used in the field mapping matches the real API name of the external ID field (including the __c suffix for custom fields) -- a typo or outdated mapping file referencing a renamed field produces this same class of error. Third, if the error specifically mentions non-uniqueness, query the Account object for duplicate values in that external ID field, since even a field correctly marked Unique will reject an upsert if the existing data already contains duplicate values that violate uniqueness.
questions.professionalAnswer: When every row fails with the same error, I treat it as a configuration problem, not a data-quality problem, and go straight to the field definition rather than inspecting individual CSV rows first. I'd open the external ID field on Account in Object Manager and confirm both the External ID and Unique checkboxes are actually checked -- it's a common setup mistake to create a field intended as an external key but forget to check External ID when creating it, which makes it look right to a human but invisible to Data Loader's relationship-mapping feature. Second, I'd open my field mapping file (the .sdl or the mapping screen) and compare the exact API name I'm referencing against the field's real API name in Setup, since a field that was renamed after the mapping was built will silently break with this same error. If the error message specifically complains about uniqueness rather than the field not existing, I'd run a quick report grouping Account by that field to find any duplicate values already sitting in the data, since Salesforce enforces true uniqueness and won't let an upsert match ambiguously against more than one record.
commonMistakes: Inspecting individual CSV data rows first instead of checking the field configuration when every row fails identically
Not verifying the field is actually marked both External ID and Unique in Setup
Not checking for an API name mismatch (especially after a field rename)
Not checking for pre-existing duplicate values when the error specifically mentions uniqueness
keyPoints: An error on every row (not just some) points to a configuration issue, not messy data
Confirm the target field is marked both External ID and Unique in Setup
Verify the exact API name in the mapping matches the field's current API name
A uniqueness-specific error often means duplicate values already exist in that field

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly reasons that an all-rows failure implies a structural/config cause
Checks the External ID/Unique field configuration
Checks for an API name mismatch
Checks for pre-existing duplicate values on a uniqueness error

lessonLink.label: Review: External IDs and Relationships During Loads

questions.title: Duplicate Accounts Keep Getting Created Despite an Active Duplicate Rule
questions.prompt: You have an active duplicate rule on Account set to Block, referencing a matching rule on Account Name. Users still report new duplicate Accounts appearing. What are the likely causes?
questions.modelAnswer: The most common cause is that the duplicate rule's Block action only applies to the channel it's configured for -- by default a duplicate rule has separate checkboxes for which contexts it runs in (standard UI, Lightning, APIs like Data Loader/the Import Wizard, and Lightning Flow), and if 'Block' is only enabled for the standard UI while records are actually being created via Data Loader or an integration using the API, the rule simply never fires for that path. A second likely cause is that the matching rule itself is too strict (requiring an exact match on a field where real duplicates have slightly different name formatting) or too narrow in which fields it compares, so genuinely duplicate records fail to match and sail through un-blocked. A third possibility is that the records are being created through an automated process (a flow, an integration, a trigger) that explicitly bypasses duplicate rules, since certain contexts and certain API-based insert methods can skip duplicate and validation checks depending on configuration.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first question is always 'how are these duplicate Accounts actually being created' -- through the UI, an integration, Data Loader, a Flow -- because duplicate rules have per-channel enablement, and a rule that blocks duplicates perfectly in the Lightning UI can be completely silent for records coming in through Data Loader or an API integration if that channel wasn't checked when the rule was configured. I'd go back into the duplicate rule's settings and confirm Block is enabled for every channel these records are actually coming through, not just assume it applies everywhere because it's marked Active. If the channels all look correctly configured, I'd pull a couple of the actual duplicate pairs users reported and manually check whether they'd really match under the existing matching rule's criteria -- often 'ABC Corp' versus 'ABC Corporation' or 'ABC Corp.' won't trigger an exact-match rule, which tells me the matching rule needs a looser or fuzzy comparison, not that the duplicate rule mechanism is broken.
commonMistakes: Assuming an active duplicate rule automatically blocks duplicates from every creation channel
Not checking which specific channels (UI, API, Flow) the rule's Block action is actually enabled for
Not examining real duplicate pairs to see if they'd actually match the existing matching rule's strictness
Not considering that an automated process might bypass duplicate checks entirely
keyPoints: Duplicate rules have per-channel enablement (UI, Lightning, API, Flow) -- a gap in one channel means no blocking there
Check which actual channel is creating the duplicates before assuming the rule mechanism is broken
Examine real duplicate examples against the matching rule's actual strictness/fields
Some automated creation paths can bypass duplicate and validation checks depending on configuration

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies per-channel enablement as a likely cause
Correctly identifies matching rule strictness as a likely cause
Considers automated/API bypass as a possibility
Frames troubleshooting around identifying the actual creation channel first

lessonLink.label: Review: Matching Rules and Duplicate Rules

questions.title: A Validation Rule Is Blocking a Legitimate Data Import
questions.prompt: A Data Loader import of 2,000 historical Opportunities is failing on about 15% of rows with a validation rule error requiring 'Close Date must not be in the past for open Opportunities.' The historical data genuinely has past close dates on records that are already Closed Won. What's going on and how do you fix the import?
questions.modelAnswer: The validation rule is almost certainly written to check close date against today's date whenever an Opportunity is open, but its condition for 'what counts as open' is probably not correctly excluding Closed Won/Closed Lost stages -- or, more likely for an import specifically, the rows are failing because the Stage value is being set in the same operation as the Close Date, and depending on row/field processing, the validation might be evaluating a transient state during the save rather than reflecting the data's true final condition. Rather than editing the live validation rule (which is the thing actually enforcing a legitimate business rule for everyday use), the safer fix for a one-time historical load is to temporarily and narrowly adjust the validation rule's logic to also check for an explicit bypass condition -- commonly, adding a custom permission or a check against the running user/profile to exempt data migration -- or, more simply, loading in a sandbox or using a dedicated 'Data Migration' permission tied to a custom permission the validation rule explicitly checks for and excludes, run the import, then remove the bypass immediately afterward.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first move is to actually open the validation rule's formula and read exactly what it checks, rather than guessing -- because 'Close Date must not be in the past for open Opportunities' sounds reasonable, but if the formula's definition of 'open' is implemented loosely (for example, checking IsClosed instead of explicitly excluding Closed Won/Closed Lost stage values, or not accounting for how Data Loader submits Stage and Close Date together), it might be misfiring on records that are actually fine. Once I understand the real formula, I would not want to just permanently loosen a validation rule that's correctly protecting day-to-day data entry -- for a one-time historical load, the right move is a temporary, scoped bypass: either a custom permission the validation rule's formula explicitly checks and skips for (assigned only to the integration user running this one-time load, then removed), or running the load in a path (like a sandbox first) where I can confirm the records truly are fine, then applying the exact same bypass approach in production for just the duration of this load. I would never want to delete or permanently weaken the validation rule as the fix, since that reopens the exact data-quality gap it exists to prevent.
commonMistakes: Permanently disabling or loosening the validation rule to get the import through
Not actually reading the validation rule's formula to understand why it's misfiring on these specific rows
Not considering a scoped bypass (custom permission check) as the correct temporary fix
Not testing the fix in a sandbox before running the real historical load in production
keyPoints: Read and understand the validation rule's actual formula logic before assuming it's simply wrong
A validation rule's definition of 'open' may not correctly exclude closed stages, or may misfire during Data Loader's field-set timing
The correct fix for a one-time load is a scoped, temporary bypass, not a permanent rule change
Remove the bypass immediately after the one-time load completes

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses by examining the actual validation rule formula
Avoids permanently weakening the validation rule
Proposes a scoped, temporary bypass mechanism
Mentions removing the bypass after the load

questions.title: A Report Is Showing Zero Rows When Data Clearly Exists
questions.prompt: A summary report on Opportunities, filtered to this quarter and the user's own team, is showing zero rows, but you can confirm matching Opportunity records definitely exist in the org. What do you check, in order?
questions.modelAnswer: First, check the report's actual filter logic rather than assuming the described filters are the only ones applied -- report filters can include a hidden or forgotten additional filter (a row-level filter left over from a previous edit), and date filters specifically are a common culprit since 'This Quarter' depends on the org's fiscal year settings, which might not align with a calendar quarter the way the viewer assumes. Second, check record-level access -- the report only shows records the running user can actually see, so if the user viewing the report doesn't have access to the Opportunities in question (due to OWD/sharing, even though the data exists), the report will legitimately show zero rows for them while an admin viewing the same report sees data. Third, confirm the report type being used actually includes the object/relationship needed -- if it's a custom report type with an overly restrictive 'each/any record' join setting between objects, qualifying Opportunities might be excluded from the report's underlying universe entirely regardless of filters.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd work through this in the order most likely to be the actual cause first. Filters first -- I'd open the report's filter logic (not just read the visible filter pills, but check the actual AND/OR logic and look for a filter that's hidden behind an 'Add filter logic' setting that isn't obvious at a glance) and specifically scrutinize the date filter, since 'This Quarter' is computed from the org's Fiscal Year settings, and if the org uses a custom fiscal year, 'this quarter' might not be the calendar quarter I assumed when checking that the data 'definitely exists.' If filters look genuinely correct, I'd check who's running the report -- if it's not me (an admin) but a regular user, their own record-level access might be the actual reason, and I'd confirm by running the report as an admin or checking the user's access to a specific qualifying Opportunity directly. Only after filters and access both check out would I dig into whether the custom report type itself is scoped in a way that excludes these records from its join entirely.
commonMistakes: Assuming the filters shown are the complete filter logic without checking for hidden/leftover conditions
Not accounting for fiscal year settings affecting what 'This Quarter' actually means
Not considering that the viewing user's own record access, not the report builder's, determines what's shown
Not considering the underlying report type's join/relationship restrictiveness as a possible cause
keyPoints: Check the report's full filter logic, not just the visible filter pills
Date filters like 'This Quarter' depend on the org's fiscal year settings
The report only shows what the viewing user can actually access -- not what exists
A custom report type's join settings can exclude qualifying records from the report entirely

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly checks full filter logic including hidden conditions
Correctly considers fiscal year impact on date filters
Correctly identifies viewer's record access as a likely cause
Considers report type join restrictiveness

questions.title: A Dashboard Is Showing Stale Numbers
questions.prompt: Users report that a dashboard is showing numbers that don't match what the underlying reports show when run directly -- the dashboard appears to be a few days behind. What's the likely cause and how do you fix it?
questions.modelAnswer: Dashboards don't run their underlying reports live every time someone views them -- they display data as of the dashboard's last refresh, which is either manual (someone clicked Refresh) or on a configured schedule, so a dashboard that looks a few days stale is almost certainly just reflecting its last scheduled or manual refresh time, visible at the top of the dashboard ('As of [date/time]'). The fix is to check the dashboard's refresh schedule (Setup/dashboard edit view, the clock or refresh icon) and either set up or correct a schedule that refreshes as often as the business actually needs, or click Refresh manually if this is a one-time check. If the dashboard is already scheduled to refresh daily and is still showing older data than expected, the next thing to check is whether the scheduled refresh is actually succeeding -- a failed scheduled refresh (often due to running-user permission issues, since dashboards refresh as whichever user is set as the dashboard's running user) will silently leave the dashboard on its last successful refresh instead of erroring visibly to every viewer.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I'd point out to a confused user is the 'As of' timestamp at the top of the dashboard -- that's the actual answer to 'why doesn't this match the report,' because a dashboard is a snapshot, not a live view, and most people genuinely don't register that distinction until it causes a visible mismatch. If there's no refresh schedule configured at all, that's an easy fix -- set one that matches how current the business actually needs this to be, daily or more often. If there IS a schedule and it's still stale, I'd check who the dashboard's running user is (a dashboard refreshes with that user's permissions and visibility, not the viewer's), and confirm that user's access or credentials haven't changed in a way that's silently causing the scheduled refresh to fail -- a deactivated running user or a permission change on their account is a classic, quiet cause of a dashboard that stops updating without any obvious error shown to the people viewing it.
commonMistakes: Assuming a dashboard automatically reflects live data the same way a report does when opened
Not checking the dashboard's 'As of' refresh timestamp as the first diagnostic step
Not knowing dashboards refresh based on a specific running user's access, not the viewer's
Not considering that a scheduled refresh might be silently failing rather than simply not being configured
keyPoints: Dashboards show a snapshot as of their last refresh, not a live view
Check the 'As of' timestamp and the refresh schedule configuration first
Dashboards refresh using a specific running user's access/permissions
A scheduled refresh can silently fail (e.g., due to the running user's access changing) without an obvious error

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the snapshot/refresh nature of dashboards
Describes checking and fixing the refresh schedule
Correctly explains the running user concept
Considers a silently failing scheduled refresh

questions.title: A Roll-Up Summary Field Isn't Updating
questions.prompt: A roll-up summary field on Account that counts related Opportunities isn't reflecting a new Opportunity you just created and verified is correctly linked to the Account. What do you check?
questions.modelAnswer: First, confirm the relationship between Opportunity and Account in this org's configuration is actually what the roll-up requires -- roll-up summary fields only work across master-detail relationships, and the standard Account-to-Opportunity relationship is a lookup, not master-detail, by default; a roll-up summary field on Account counting Opportunities is only possible if this is a custom scenario with a genuine master-detail relationship, or if the count is actually being done some other way (a formula, a flow, a scheduled process) that's being mistaken for a native roll-up. Second, assuming it is a genuine master-detail setup, check the roll-up field's filter criteria -- the new Opportunity might simply not meet a filter condition the roll-up applies (for example, a filter requiring Stage not equal to a certain value, or requiring a specific Record Type), so it's correctly excluded rather than broken. Third, consider whether the field value is cached in a view the user hasn't refreshed, or whether there's a delay from a recent bulk operation still processing in the background.
questions.professionalAnswer: The very first thing I'd verify, because it's the thing most likely to be wrong in this exact scenario, is whether this relationship is actually master-detail at all -- native Account-Opportunity in standard Salesforce is a lookup relationship, which structurally cannot support a roll-up summary field. If someone built what they're calling a 'roll-up' here, it might actually be a formula field, a Flow-based counter, or an Apex trigger-maintained field, each of which has entirely different troubleshooting steps than a native roll-up. Assuming I'm wrong and this really is master-detail (perhaps via a custom object standing in for the relationship), I'd then check the roll-up's own filter criteria on the field definition -- it's very possible the new Opportunity doesn't meet whatever condition the roll-up filters on, which would mean the roll-up is actually working correctly and just not counting this particular record for a legitimate reason. I'd confirm by temporarily removing the filter criteria (in a sandbox, not production) and seeing if the count then includes the new record, which tells me definitively whether it's a filter issue or something else.
commonMistakes: Assuming the field must be a native roll-up without verifying the relationship is actually master-detail
Not checking the roll-up's own filter criteria as a likely, legitimate reason for exclusion
Not considering the field might actually be formula/Flow/Apex-maintained rather than a native roll-up
Jumping to 'it's broken' without testing whether removing filter criteria changes the behavior
keyPoints: Roll-up summary fields require a genuine master-detail relationship -- verify this isn't actually a lookup
The field might not be a native roll-up at all (could be formula, Flow, or Apex-maintained)
Check the roll-up's filter criteria -- the new record may be correctly excluded
Test by temporarily adjusting filter criteria in a sandbox to isolate the cause

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly questions whether this is truly a native master-detail roll-up
Correctly checks filter criteria as a likely legitimate cause
Considers alternative implementations (formula/Flow/Apex)
Proposes a concrete test to isolate the cause

questions.title: A Bulk Delete of Parent Records Took Child Records With It Unexpectedly
questions.prompt: An admin bulk-deleted 50 'obsolete' Service Order records via Data Loader, and now 300 Warranty Claim records tied to those orders are also gone, which nobody realized would happen. What happened, and how do you both recover and prevent a repeat?
questions.modelAnswer: This is the cascading-delete behavior inherent to master-detail relationships -- since Warranty Claim is the detail record to Service Order's master, deleting a master record deletes every associated detail record automatically; this isn't a bug or a Data Loader quirk, it's the defined behavior of the relationship type the schema was built with. For recovery, first check the Recycle Bin -- both the deleted Service Orders and the cascaded Warranty Claims typically land there together (not permanently erased) and can be restored via Data Loader's query against deleted records or the UI's Recycle Bin restore, though restoring the parent generally restores its details together, so this should recover most or all of it if done soon (before the Recycle Bin's retention period or storage limit purges them). For prevention, going forward: before any bulk delete of master records, explicitly query and review how many detail records would be affected, and consider whether 'obsolete' records should instead be handled via an archival approach (a status field, excluding them from active views) rather than actual deletion when cascading loss hasn't been reviewed.
questions.professionalAnswer: The underlying mechanism is exactly what master-detail relationships are supposed to do -- Warranty Claim can't exist without its Service Order by the nature of the relationship, so deleting the master necessarily takes its details with it; the admin's mistake wasn't a technical error, it was not realizing (or not checking) that this relationship was master-detail and what that implies before running a bulk delete. For recovery, my first move is the Recycle Bin -- Salesforce typically retains deleted records (parent and cascaded children together) for a window before permanent erasure, so I'd go look there immediately rather than assuming the data is gone, and if volume is awkward for the UI I'd use Data Loader's 'query for deleted records' capability to pull and restore them in bulk. Once recovered, the actual prevention conversation is about process: before any bulk delete touching a master-detail parent, I'd want a quick check -- a report or query counting related detail records -- built into the delete process itself, so nobody runs a 50-record 'small cleanup' delete without seeing upfront that it's actually a 300-record impact.
commonMistakes: Treating the cascading delete as a bug rather than expected master-detail behavior
Not checking the Recycle Bin first, assuming the data is permanently gone
Not proposing a concrete process change (pre-delete impact check) to prevent recurrence
Not considering an archival/status-flag alternative to actual deletion for 'obsolete' records
keyPoints: Cascading delete is expected, defined behavior for master-detail relationships, not a bug
The Recycle Bin usually retains both parent and cascaded child records together for a retention window
Data Loader can query and restore deleted records in bulk when volume is high
Prevention requires a pre-delete impact check and/or an archival alternative to deletion

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains cascading delete as expected master-detail behavior
Correctly proposes Recycle Bin recovery as the first step
Proposes a concrete prevention process
Mentions an archival alternative to deletion

lessonLink.label: Review: Recycle Bin and Data Recovery

questions.title: Designing a Profile and Permission Set Strategy for a New Org
questions.prompt: You're setting up security from scratch for a 200-user org spanning Sales, Support, and Marketing, each with two or three sub-roles. How would you decide how many profiles to create versus how much to handle with permission sets?
questions.modelAnswer: The architectural principle is: profiles should map to the small number of genuinely distinct baseline access patterns (broadly, what apps, record types, and core object CRUD a user needs just to do their job's core function), and permission sets should handle everything that varies within or across those baselines -- extra object access, a specific feature, a temporary project need. For three departments with two or three sub-roles each, that doesn't mean 9 profiles; it likely means somewhere around 3-5 profiles (one per department, possibly splitting Sales into two if the baseline CRUD genuinely differs between, say, a rep and a sales ops person) with permission sets and permission set groups layered on top to handle the sub-role variation -- a 'Sales Ops Extras' permission set, a 'Team Lead Reporting Access' permission set, bundled into groups per sub-role so assignment stays a one-click action per person.
questions.professionalAnswer: My starting question for every sub-role is 'does this group need a genuinely different floor of access, or just a bit more on top of a floor another group already has?' Most sub-role variation I've seen in practice is additive -- a Senior Support Agent needing one more object than a regular Support Agent, not needing a fundamentally different set of apps or tabs -- which is exactly what permission sets are for, not a reason to fork a new profile. I'd design around 3 to 5 profiles total here, matching real baseline differences (Sales, Support, Marketing, and maybe a split within Sales if reps and ops are structurally different enough), and then build a permission set per distinct 'extra capability,' bundled into permission set groups named after the actual sub-role so an admin assigns one group per new hire instead of hunting for the right combination of individual permission sets. I'd actively resist the pressure to create a profile per sub-role just because it feels like a one-to-one mapping to the org chart -- that's the pattern that leads to profile sprawl and a security model nobody can audit two years later.
commonMistakes: Defaulting to one profile per sub-role, leading to profile sprawl
Not distinguishing genuine baseline differences from additive extras when deciding profile count
Not using permission set groups to keep assignment simple despite having more granular permission sets
Designing security reactively per request instead of around a deliberate small set of baselines
keyPoints: Profiles should map to genuinely distinct baseline access patterns, not every sub-role
Permission sets handle additive variation within or across baselines
Permission set groups keep assignment simple even with many granular permission sets
Profile sprawl (one per sub-role) becomes an audit and maintenance liability over time

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly articulates the baseline-vs-additive distinction
Proposes a realistic, small profile count with justification
Describes using permission sets/groups for sub-role variation
Names profile sprawl as the risk being avoided

questions.title: Combining OWD, Role Hierarchy, and Sharing Rules Into One Security Design
questions.prompt: Design the record-level security approach for a Case object where: support agents should see only their own team's cases by default, team leads should see their whole team's cases, and a small Compliance group needs to see every case regardless of team, but only read-only. Walk through your layered design.
questions.modelAnswer: Layer one, OWD: set Case to Private, establishing that nobody sees another team's cases by default. Layer two, role hierarchy: structure roles so each team's agents report up to that team's lead (Support Agent - Team A under Team Lead - Team A, and so on), which automatically gives team leads visibility into their own team's cases without any additional sharing rule, since that's exactly what hierarchy rollup provides. Layer three, for Compliance (which isn't part of the support role hierarchy at all and needs cross-team visibility that hierarchy alone can't express), add a role-based or public-group-based sharing rule granting the Compliance group Read Only access to Cases owned by any support role -- since Compliance sits outside the team structure, this has to be an explicit sharing rule rather than relying on hierarchy position. The three layers compose cleanly: OWD sets the floor, hierarchy handles the natural management rollup, and the sharing rule handles the one cross-cutting exception that doesn't fit the hierarchy's shape.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd design this top-down through the layers rather than trying to solve it with one mechanism. Private OWD is non-negotiable as the starting point, since 'agents see only their team by default' literally requires a restrictive baseline -- nothing wider would correctly exclude other teams. Then the team lead visibility requirement is a textbook role hierarchy use case: if I structure a role per team with agents beneath their lead, the lead's upward visibility into their team's cases comes for free, with zero sharing rules needed for that specific relationship -- trying to solve team-lead visibility with a sharing rule instead would be redundant and harder to maintain as teams change. Compliance is the interesting piece precisely because they don't fit anywhere in that hierarchy -- they're not above any specific team, they're orthogonal to the whole structure -- so a sharing rule naming the Compliance public group as the recipient, scoped to all Cases (criteria-based with essentially no restrictive filter, or owner-based naming every support role), access level Read Only, is the right tool specifically because hierarchy can't express 'see across every branch but don't manage any of them.'
commonMistakes: Trying to solve team-lead visibility with a sharing rule instead of relying on role hierarchy
Not recognizing Compliance's cross-cutting need doesn't fit the hierarchy and requires a sharing rule
Starting from a wider-than-Private OWD and trying to restrict down later
Granting Compliance more than Read Only when the requirement specifically limits them to read-only
keyPoints: OWD Private establishes the restrictive baseline all three requirements build on
Role hierarchy (team structure under team leads) handles team-lead rollup automatically
A sharing rule is the correct tool for Compliance's cross-cutting, non-hierarchical need
Each layer is used for what it's actually suited to, not forced to do another layer's job

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly sets OWD to Private as the foundation
Correctly uses role hierarchy for team-lead visibility, not a sharing rule
Correctly uses a sharing rule for Compliance's cross-cutting need
Respects the Read Only constraint for Compliance

questions.title: When Permission Sets Alone Aren't Enough at Scale
questions.prompt: Your org has grown to the point where a handful of 'super user' employees each need a unique, slightly different combination of 20+ permission sets, hand-assigned one by one, and it's become unmanageable to track who has what. What's your architectural fix?
questions.modelAnswer: The fix is introducing permission set groups as an intermediate abstraction layer between individual permission sets and users -- instead of hand-assigning 20+ individual permission sets per super user, define the actual recurring combinations (or near-combinations) as named groups that represent real job functions ('Senior Support Lead Bundle,' 'Regional Ops Bundle'), using muting permission sets inside each group to handle the small per-group exceptions, so that assigning or auditing a user's access becomes 'which 1-3 groups are they in' instead of 'which 20 of 40 possible permission sets are they in.' If even after grouping there's still genuine one-off variation that doesn't fit any group well, that specific user gets their group assignment plus one or two individual permission sets layered on top for their unique sliver -- but the goal is for individual-permission-set assignment to become the rare exception, not the default pattern for everyone.
questions.professionalAnswer: When I see 20+ individually hand-assigned permission sets per user, my first reaction is that nobody has stepped back to ask what the actual recurring combinations are -- some of those 20 are probably shared by every 'super user,' and if I can identify that common core, that becomes one permission set group right there, cutting the per-user assignment list dramatically. I'd actually go pull every super user's current assignment list, diff them against each other, and look for the real clusters -- if 8 of 10 super users share the same 15 permission sets and only differ on the remaining 5, that's a strong signal for one base group (the shared 15) plus one or two smaller groups or muting permission sets for the differences, rather than 10 individually tracked snowflake users. The deeper architectural point is that at 20+ individually assigned permission sets, auditing 'what can this person actually do' has become practically impossible without opening their user record and manually cross-referencing each one -- permission set groups aren't just a convenience, they're what makes the access model auditable again.
commonMistakes: Proposing to just keep hand-assigning permission sets more carefully instead of introducing groups
Not identifying the actual recurring combinations before designing groups
Not mentioning muting permission sets for handling per-group exceptions
Missing the auditability argument -- treating this as purely an assignment-convenience problem
keyPoints: Permission set groups are the right abstraction when recurring 20+ permission set combinations become unmanageable
Identify real recurring clusters across current users before designing groups
Muting permission sets handle small per-group exceptions without new individual permission sets
The deeper problem being solved is auditability, not just assignment convenience

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly proposes permission set groups as the architectural fix
Describes identifying real recurring clusters from current assignments
Mentions muting permission sets for exceptions
Articulates the auditability benefit, not just convenience

questions.title: Designing a Data Load Strategy for a Multi-Object Migration
questions.prompt: You're migrating Accounts, Contacts, and Opportunities from a legacy system into Salesforce, where Opportunities reference Contacts as the primary contact, and Contacts reference Accounts. Design the load sequence and strategy.
questions.modelAnswer: The load has to respect the dependency order: Accounts first (no dependencies), then Contacts (depend on Accounts existing), then Opportunities (depend on both Accounts and Contacts existing), since you can't link a child to a parent that doesn't exist in Salesforce yet. Each object should have a dedicated External ID field populated with the legacy system's own identifier, so each load stage can use upsert and resolve relationships (Contact to Account, Opportunity to Contact/Account) purely by the legacy keys already present in the source data, without a manual ID cross-reference step between stages. The strategy should also include a validation checkpoint between each stage -- after loading Accounts, confirm the count and spot-check a sample before moving to Contacts, since an error at the Account stage (missing records, bad external IDs) will cascade into failed or mis-linked Contacts and Opportunities if not caught first.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd sequence this strictly by dependency: Accounts, then Contacts, then Opportunities, and I wouldn't try to parallelize or reorder that for speed, because any shortcut here just produces unresolved relationship errors I'd have to redo anyway. Before touching any load, I'd make sure every one of the three objects has its own External ID field tied to the legacy system's identifier -- Account gets Legacy_Account_Id__c, Contact gets Legacy_Contact_Id__c, and so on -- so that at each stage, Data Loader can resolve the parent relationship directly from the source file's own legacy keys rather than me building manual Salesforce-ID cross-reference tables between stages. After each stage, I'd stop and validate before moving on -- row counts matching expectations, a handful of spot-checked records with their relationships actually correct -- because Opportunities being the last and most dependent stage means any quietly broken Account or Contact data compounds into Opportunity-stage failures that are much more annoying to untangle after the fact than catching the root cause one stage earlier. I'd also plan the whole thing with a full sandbox dry run of all three stages before touching production, specifically to surface dependency-order mistakes somewhere consequence-free.
commonMistakes: Attempting to load Opportunities, Contacts, and Accounts in the wrong order or in parallel
Not setting up External ID fields on all three objects before starting
Not validating each stage before proceeding to the next, letting errors compound
Skipping a full sandbox dry run before the production migration
keyPoints: Load order must respect dependencies: Accounts, then Contacts, then Opportunities
Each object needs its own External ID field tied to the legacy system's key
Validate each stage's results before proceeding, since errors compound downstream
A full sandbox dry run surfaces sequencing and mapping mistakes before production

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly sequences the three-object load by dependency
Correctly proposes External ID fields on all three objects
Includes stage-by-stage validation
Mentions a sandbox dry run

questions.title: Choosing an External ID Strategy Across Multiple Integrations
questions.prompt: Your org integrates with three different external systems (an ERP, a marketing platform, and a legacy CRM being retired), and all three need to reference the same Account records. How would you architect the External ID fields to support this long-term, not just for one migration?
questions.modelAnswer: Rather than a single shared external ID field, the right long-term architecture is one dedicated External ID field per source system (ERP_Account_Id__c, Marketing_Platform_Account_Id__c, Legacy_CRM_Account_Id__c), each marked External ID (and Unique where the source guarantees uniqueness), because conflating multiple systems' identifiers into one field risks collisions (two different systems coincidentally using the same identifier format or value) and makes it impossible to tell, later, which system a given value actually came from. This also supports the legacy CRM's eventual retirement cleanly -- that field can simply stop being updated and, eventually, be deprecated or archived without affecting the still-active ERP and marketing platform integrations, since each system's mapping is fully independent. Each integration (not a human) should own writing to and relying on its own field, keeping the ongoing sync logic for each system isolated from the others.
questions.professionalAnswer: My default architecture here is one External ID field per source system, never a shared one, because the moment two systems are forced to use the same field, I lose the ability to know unambiguously which system a given value represents, and I open the door to a genuine collision if both systems happen to generate overlapping identifier values or formats. So I'd create ERP_Account_Id__c, Marketing_Platform_Account_Id__c, and Legacy_CRM_Account_Id__c, each independently marked External ID, and have each integration's sync process reference only its own field for upsert matching -- the ERP integration never looks at or writes to the marketing platform's field, and vice versa. This pays off specifically with the legacy CRM retirement mentioned in the question: because that system's field is fully independent, retiring it is just a matter of stopping writes to Legacy_CRM_Account_Id__c (and eventually removing the field) with zero risk to the ERP or marketing platform's still-active integrations, which would not be true if all three had been sharing one overloaded external ID field from the start.
commonMistakes: Proposing a single shared External ID field for all three systems
Not considering the collision risk of overlapping identifier formats/values across systems
Not addressing how this design supports the legacy CRM's eventual retirement cleanly
Not marking the appropriate fields as Unique where the source system guarantees it
keyPoints: Use one dedicated External ID field per source system, not a shared field
A shared field risks identifier collisions and loses clarity about which system a value came from
Independent fields let one integration be retired without affecting the others
Each integration should read/write only its own field

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly proposes one External ID field per source system
Explains the collision/ambiguity risk of a shared field
Connects the design to the legacy system's clean retirement
Notes each integration should own only its own field
