questions.title: Designing a Report Folder and Custom Report Type Structure
questions.prompt: As the org grows past 300 reports with no real organization, you're asked to design a sustainable report folder and custom report type structure for Sales, Support, and Marketing. What's your approach?
questions.modelAnswer: For folders, the architecture should be organized primarily by audience/department with clear sharing boundaries (Sales Reports, Support Reports, Marketing Reports, plus a Shared/Executive folder for cross-department views), each folder's sharing set explicitly (view/edit/manage access tied to the relevant public groups or roles) rather than left at defaults, so reports don't end up either invisible to the people who need them or visible to everyone regardless of relevance. For custom report types, the approach should be building a small, deliberate set that reflects genuinely recurring reporting needs spanning standard report types' limits -- for example, an Opportunity-with-Line-Items-and-Account-fields custom report type if that combination is requested often -- rather than letting individual users create one-off custom report types ad hoc, since an unmanaged proliferation of custom report types is exactly how an org ends up with 300+ overlapping reports in the first place. Both efforts should be paired with a cleanup pass identifying and archiving/deleting genuinely unused existing reports before imposing new structure on top of the mess.
questions.professionalAnswer: Before building any new structure, I'd actually audit what exists -- which of the 300 reports are run regularly versus never touched, because imposing a beautiful new folder structure on top of 300 reports without first retiring the dead ones just creates a well-organized mess instead of an unorganized one. Once I have a sense of what's actually in active use, I'd design folders around departments with real audiences in mind, and critically, actually set each folder's sharing explicitly rather than leaving it at an org default -- 'Sales Reports' should be genuinely visible to Sales and not just technically existing in a folder nobody configured access to. For custom report types, my rule is that a new one gets created because multiple people keep needing the same unusual combination of objects/fields that standard report types can't provide, not because one person once wanted it -- I'd actually ask requesters to justify a new custom report type against that bar rather than approving every request, since each unreviewed custom report type is one more long-term maintenance surface and a likely source of 'why are there three almost-identical reports' problems down the line.
commonMistakes: Designing new folder structure without first auditing and retiring genuinely unused reports
Leaving folder sharing at default instead of explicitly configuring it per audience
Creating custom report types reactively for every individual request without a recurring-need bar
Not considering cross-department/executive reporting needs in the folder design
keyPoints: Audit and retire unused reports before imposing new structure on the existing mess
Design folders around real audiences with sharing explicitly configured, not left at default
Only create new custom report types for genuinely recurring needs standard types can't meet
Include a cross-department/executive folder for reports spanning multiple areas

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Proposes an audit/cleanup pass before restructuring
Correctly designs folder structure with explicit sharing
Proposes a deliberate bar for new custom report types
Addresses cross-department reporting needs

questions.title: Designing Dashboards for Different Audiences from the Same Data
questions.prompt: Leadership wants one dashboard experience that works for a VP (who wants company-wide numbers), a Regional Manager (who wants just their region), and an individual rep (who wants just their own numbers) -- without building and maintaining three separate dashboards. What's your architecture?
questions.modelAnswer: The right tool is a Dynamic Dashboard, where the dashboard's running user is set to 'View dashboard as logged-in user' rather than a single fixed running user -- this means each viewer sees the data filtered to their own actual record-level access (via the normal OWD/role hierarchy/sharing model) rather than everyone seeing the same fixed running user's view. Built on top of reports with Opportunity Owner or Region-driven access already correctly scoped through sharing, a VP whose role sits atop the hierarchy sees everything, a Regional Manager whose role covers their region's reps sees just that region, and a rep sees just their own records -- all from the exact same single dashboard and underlying reports, with zero per-audience duplication, because the dashboard isn't encoding the audience difference at all; the org's existing record-level security model is doing that work automatically through who's logged in.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first move is recognizing this isn't really a dashboard-design problem, it's a 'does the underlying record-level security already reflect these three audiences correctly' problem -- if the role hierarchy and sharing model are already set up so a rep sees only their own Opportunities, a regional manager sees their region's, and the VP sees everything (which is exactly the kind of hierarchy-driven access we'd want anyway), then a single Dynamic Dashboard set to run as the logged-in viewer gets this behavior essentially for free. I'd build the dashboard once, make sure its underlying reports aren't hard-filtered to one specific region or rep (that would defeat the whole point), and set it to Dynamic/logged-in-user mode rather than a fixed running user. Then I'd test by logging in (or using 'Login As') as a representative user from each of the three audience tiers and confirming each one sees exactly the scope they should -- which is really a verification that the security model is correct, since the dashboard itself isn't doing any audience-specific logic at all.
commonMistakes: Proposing three separate dashboards instead of one dynamic dashboard
Not knowing Dynamic Dashboards support a 'logged-in user' running user mode
Hard-filtering the underlying reports to one audience, defeating the dynamic approach
Not recognizing this is fundamentally a record-level security correctness question, not a dashboard feature question
keyPoints: A single Dynamic Dashboard, run as the logged-in user, serves all three audiences at once
The underlying reports must not be hard-filtered to one audience's data
Correct behavior depends on the org's existing role hierarchy/sharing model being accurate
Test with representative users from each tier to confirm correct scoping

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly proposes a Dynamic Dashboard with logged-in-user running user
Correctly explains why underlying reports must stay unfiltered by audience
Connects correct behavior to the existing security model
Describes a sensible multi-user verification approach

questions.title: Lookup vs. Master-Detail as an Architectural Decision for a New Custom Object
questions.prompt: You're designing a 'Site Visit' custom object that will always relate to exactly one 'Property' custom object record. The business says reporting roll-ups (count/sum of visits per property) are important, but they also mention that occasionally a Site Visit needs to be reassigned to a different Property after the fact, and Property records are sometimes archived (not deleted) while their Site Visits must remain visible. How do you decide the relationship type?
questions.modelAnswer: This is a genuine tradeoff rather than an obvious choice: master-detail would give the roll-up summary for free but makes reassignment to a different Property harder (reparenting a master-detail child requires the relationship field to allow reparenting, which isn't the default and has its own constraints) and ties Site Visit's fate to Property's -- if a Property were ever deleted, its Site Visits would cascade-delete too, which conflicts with the stated need for Site Visits to remain visible even when a Property is archived (though 'archived,' not deleted, actually sidesteps the cascading-delete risk specifically). Given reassignment is described as needed and cascading-delete risk exists if Property is ever actually deleted, a defensible architecture is Lookup plus a separate roll-up mechanism (a Flow or a scheduled process maintaining a count/sum field on Property) -- trading the free native roll-up for the flexibility and safety the business's other two requirements actually call for; if reassignment turns out to be rare enough to tolerate master-detail's reparenting friction, master-detail with reparenting enabled is the other legitimate answer, provided deletion of Property is governed carefully (e.g., using archiving, never hard delete).
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through each requirement and check it against both relationship types rather than defaulting straight to master-detail just because roll-ups are mentioned. Roll-up favors master-detail, clearly. But reassignment to a different Property after the fact is the one that gives me pause -- master-detail does support reparenting, but it has to be explicitly enabled on the field and comes with its own rules (like requiring the same record type/sharing), so it's not as frictionless as a lookup's reparenting, which just means updating a lookup value. And the archived-but-visible requirement actually tells me the real danger isn't archiving (archived Property records still exist, so master-detail's cascading delete wouldn't even trigger) -- it's if anyone ever actually deletes a Property, which would take its Site Visits with it under master-detail, directly contradicting 'Site Visits must remain visible.' Given that mix, I'd lean toward Lookup with a Flow-maintained roll-up field on Property, explicitly trading away the free native roll-up for safety against an accidental Property deletion and simpler reassignment -- but I'd say this out loud as a real tradeoff decision to the business, not present it as the only possible answer, since reasonable teams could land on reparenting-enabled master-detail instead if reassignment turns out to be rare.
commonMistakes: Defaulting to master-detail purely because roll-up summaries were mentioned, without weighing the other two requirements
Not knowing master-detail relationships can support reparenting if explicitly enabled
Confusing archiving (record still exists) with deletion (triggers cascading delete) as the actual risk
Presenting the decision as obvious/one-size-fits-all instead of a genuine tradeoff with a stated rationale
keyPoints: Master-detail gives free roll-ups but complicates reassignment and risks cascading delete
Lookup avoids cascading-delete risk and simplifies reassignment but needs a separate roll-up mechanism
Archiving (not deleting) a Property sidesteps cascading delete even under master-detail
This is a genuine architectural tradeoff -- a defensible answer explains the reasoning, not just picks one

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the roll-up vs. reassignment vs. deletion-risk tradeoff
Correctly explains reparenting rules for master-detail
Correctly distinguishes archiving from deletion as the real risk factor
Presents a reasoned recommendation while acknowledging it's a genuine tradeoff

questions.title: Designing a Junction Object for a Many-to-Many Relationship
questions.prompt: The business wants Contacts to be associated with multiple Projects, and Projects to have multiple Contacts, each association carrying its own 'Role on Project' value (like Sponsor, Technical Lead). Design the data model.
questions.modelAnswer: A direct many-to-many isn't representable with a single lookup or master-detail field, since each of those only models a one-to-many; the standard pattern is a junction object -- a new custom object, something like 'Project Contact Role,' with two master-detail (or one master-detail and one lookup, depending on which side should control cascading behavior and roll-ups) relationship fields, one to Contact and one to Project. Each row in this junction object represents one specific Contact-Project pairing, and because it's its own object, it can carry additional fields beyond just the two relationships -- exactly where 'Role on Project' belongs, as a picklist field on the junction object itself, not forced awkwardly onto either Contact or Project where it wouldn't make sense (a Contact can have a different role on each different Project). This also naturally supports roll-up summaries on either side (count of Projects per Contact, or count/list of Contacts per Project) if both relationship fields are master-detail.
questions.professionalAnswer: The moment the business says 'multiple on both sides, plus some extra information about each specific pairing,' that's the exact signature of a junction object, so I'd design a new custom object -- 'Project Contact Role' -- sitting between Contact and Project with two relationship fields, one to each. I'd lean toward making both master-detail if there's no strong reason not to, since that gives me roll-up summaries for free on both sides (a count of active Projects per Contact, a count of Contacts per Project) and keeps the junction records' lifecycle tied appropriately to their parents. The 'Role on Project' field goes directly on this junction object as a picklist, which is the clean answer to a detail that's genuinely per-pairing, not per-Contact or per-Project -- if I tried to put it on Contact instead, I'd have no way to represent a Contact who's a Sponsor on one Project and a Technical Lead on another, since a field on Contact can only hold one value regardless of how many Projects that Contact touches.
commonMistakes: Trying to model the many-to-many with a single lookup/master-detail field instead of a junction object
Putting 'Role on Project' on Contact or Project directly instead of on the junction object
Not considering master-detail (for roll-up capability) as the relationship type on the junction object's two fields
Not explaining why a per-pairing attribute specifically requires its own object rather than either parent
keyPoints: A many-to-many relationship requires a junction object with two relationship fields
Per-pairing attributes (like Role on Project) belong on the junction object, not either parent
Master-detail on both junction relationships typically enables useful roll-up summaries on both sides
A field on either parent object can't represent a value that varies per relationship instance

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly proposes a junction object design
Correctly places the per-pairing attribute on the junction object
Discusses relationship type choice (master-detail) and roll-up implications
Explains why the attribute can't live on either parent object

lessonLink.label: Review: Many-to-Many Relationships and Junction Objects

questions.title: Record Type and Page Layout Architecture Across Business Units
questions.prompt: A company with three business units (Residential, Commercial, Government) all sell through the same Opportunity object, but each unit has different required fields, different stage names for part of their process, and different user populations who should only see their own unit's layout. Design the record type and layout architecture.
questions.modelAnswer: Create one record type per business unit (Residential Opportunity, Commercial Opportunity, Government Opportunity), each tied to its own sales process if stage names genuinely differ per unit (Salesforce supports multiple sales processes, each with its own picklist value set for Stage, assigned to a specific record type) -- this handles the 'different stage names for part of their process' requirement correctly at the process level rather than trying to fake it with a generic Stage field and hope everyone uses the right subset. Build a dedicated page layout per business unit reflecting each one's actually-different required fields. Then, in the Page Layout Assignment matrix, map each business unit's profile(s) to their own record type's layout, and critically, use record type-level profile assignment (which profiles can even use/select which record type at all) so a Residential user isn't even offered the Commercial or Government record type as an option when creating an Opportunity, keeping the experience clean rather than just relying on layout differences for users who could technically pick any record type.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd build this as three parallel tracks -- record type, sales process, and layout -- per business unit, rather than trying to solve 'different fields and different stages' with just layouts, since Stage value differences specifically need their own sales process, not just a layout change (a page layout doesn't change which picklist values are available, only which fields/sections show). So: three sales processes if the stage names genuinely diverge, three record types each tied to the matching process, three page layouts with each unit's actually-relevant required fields, and then the full Profile x Record Type assignment matrix wired so each business unit's profile only ever sees its own unit's layout. The detail I'd insist on besides the layout assignment is restricting record type availability itself at the profile level -- without that, a Residential rep could technically still select 'Commercial Opportunity' from the record type picker even though they'd never need to, which is both confusing and a minor data-integrity risk if they pick the wrong one by accident. Getting all three business units cleanly separated this way also means a future fourth business unit is a known, repeatable pattern to add, not a one-off scramble.
commonMistakes: Trying to handle different stage names with a layout change instead of a separate sales process
Not restricting record type availability per profile, letting users select units they shouldn't
Building only layouts without the matching record types and sales processes
Not designing the solution as a repeatable pattern for a future additional business unit
keyPoints: Different Stage values per unit require separate sales processes, not just layout changes
Each business unit needs its own record type, sales process, and page layout, properly linked
Record type availability should be restricted per profile, not just controlled via layout assignment
A clean three-part design per unit creates a repeatable pattern for future business units

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly separates sales process (Stage values) from page layout concerns
Correctly designs record type + layout + assignment per business unit
Includes restricting record type availability at the profile level
Notes the design's repeatability for future business units

lessonLink.label: Review: Record Types and Business Processes

questions.title: Explaining a Permission Change to a Non-Technical Stakeholder
questions.prompt: You need to tighten a profile's permissions to fix a security gap, which will remove an ability a department head didn't realize their team had (and didn't actually need). How do you explain this change to them before making it?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer leads with the business reason, not the technical mechanism -- explaining what risk the current setup creates in plain terms (for example, 'your team can currently permanently delete records that other departments rely on, which isn't something they've needed to do and creates a real risk if it happens by accident') before mentioning profiles, permission sets, or any Salesforce-specific terminology the department head doesn't need to evaluate the decision. It's also honest about the fact that this is a genuine change to their team's current capability, not a neutral background fix, and proactively checks whether anyone on the team actually does rely on that ability for a reason the admin doesn't know about, rather than assuming the audit is complete and announcing the change as already decided. If someone does need it, the answer should describe restoring that one person's access narrowly (a permission set) rather than abandoning the fix for the whole team.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd open with the actual risk in business language, not Salesforce jargon: 'I found that your team currently has the ability to permanently delete Opportunity records, and nobody's used it as far as I can tell, but if it happened by accident, there'd be no way to get that data back -- I'd like to remove that ability from your team's standard access.' That's something a department head can actually evaluate without knowing what a profile is. I'd also ask directly whether anyone on the team does use that ability for something I might not be aware of, because the whole point of checking in first instead of just making the change is catching a real exception before it becomes an outage. If it turns out one specific person does need it for a legitimate reason, I'd say so and describe the fix precisely -- 'I'll keep it removed for the team generally and add it back just for [person], since they're the one who actually uses it' -- rather than either overriding my own fix because one person objected, or ignoring a legitimate need I didn't know about.
commonMistakes: Leading with technical terminology (profiles, permission sets) instead of the actual business risk
Announcing the change as already decided instead of checking for a legitimate exception first
Abandoning the whole fix because one person pushes back, instead of scoping a narrow exception
Not explaining why the current setup is actually risky, leaving the stakeholder unable to evaluate the decision
keyPoints: Lead with the business risk in plain language, not technical mechanism
Proactively check for a legitimate, unknown exception before announcing the change as final
If an exception exists, scope it narrowly (a permission set) rather than abandoning the broader fix
Be transparent that this is a real capability change, not a neutral background adjustment

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Explains the change in plain business language, not jargon
Proactively checks for a legitimate exception before finalizing
Proposes scoping any real exception narrowly rather than abandoning the fix
Is honest and transparent rather than minimizing the change

questions.title: A Manager Asks for Access That Seems Too Broad
questions.prompt: Your manager asks you to grant a contractor 'the same access as a System Administrator, just to be safe, so we don't have to deal with access requests during this project.' You're not comfortable with that. How do you handle it?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer doesn't simply refuse or simply comply -- it treats this as a case where the requester (the manager) likely hasn't thought through the actual risk of unrestricted contractor access, and the right response is to surface that risk concretely and propose a scoped alternative, rather than framing the pushback as 'no' without an alternative, which tends to just create friction without solving the manager's real underlying concern (wanting the project to move without access friction). The answer should name the specific risk of full admin access for a contractor -- a non-employee having the ability to see and modify every record and every security setting org-wide, including other departments' sensitive data entirely unrelated to the contractor's project -- and offer to build a permission set (or set) covering exactly what the project genuinely requires, explicitly committing to turn around additional access requests quickly if something's missing, which directly addresses the manager's stated motivation (avoiding access-request friction) without the blanket risk.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't just say 'I can't do that' and leave it there, because my manager's actual goal -- not having this project get stuck waiting on access requests -- is reasonable, even if the specific ask isn't the right way to achieve it. I'd say something like, 'I get wanting to avoid access friction during the project, but giving a contractor full System Administrator access means they could see and change things completely unrelated to this project -- other departments' data, security settings, everything -- and that's a real risk for a non-employee, not just a formality. Let me build a permission set that covers everything I can tell this project actually needs, and if something's missing, I'll turn around the fix same-day so we're not actually losing the speed you're trying to protect.' That reframes it from 'I'm blocking you' to 'I'm solving the same problem you're trying to solve, just without the exposure,' which is usually what actually gets a manager to agree, rather than digging in on a request they made somewhat reflexively.
commonMistakes: Simply refusing without proposing a scoped alternative that addresses the manager's actual concern
Simply complying because a manager asked, without raising the real risk
Not naming the specific risk concretely (what a contractor with full admin access could actually do)
Framing the response as pure pushback instead of addressing the manager's underlying motivation
keyPoints: Address the manager's real underlying concern (avoiding access friction), not just the literal request
Name the specific risk of unrestricted non-employee access concretely
Propose a scoped permission set as the alternative, not a flat refusal
Commit to fast turnaround on additional access needs to preserve project speed

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Addresses the manager's underlying motivation, not just refuses
Names the specific security risk concretely
Proposes a scoped, concrete alternative (permission set)
Commits to responsiveness to avoid reintroducing the friction problem

questions.title: Communicating a Data Cleanup Plan Before a Big Deduplication Project
questions.prompt: You're about to run a large-scale account deduplication/merge project that will affect thousands of records across multiple departments. How do you communicate this before you start, and what do you do if a department pushes back partway through?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer treats upfront, specific communication as a requirement, not a courtesy -- explaining to every affected department, before starting, roughly how many of their records will be affected, what 'merge' actually does to data they might not expect (that a losing record's unique related data needs a clear survivorship rule, and some related records might move, get hidden, or require review), and giving them a real window to flag records they believe shouldn't be merged, rather than announcing the project is already underway. It should also describe a reversible, staged approach (processing in batches, keeping a backup/export before each batch, starting with a lower-risk department first) rather than running the entire merge as one irreversible action, specifically so a mid-project pushback from one department can be addressed by pausing and investigating rather than having already broken something unrecoverable.
questions.professionalAnswer: Before I'd run anything, I'd go to every affected department with specifics, not a vague 'we're cleaning up account data' notice -- something like 'our dedup process has identified roughly 400 of your accounts as likely duplicates; here's what a merge actually does to related records, and here's how you can flag any of these you believe aren't actually duplicates before we touch them.' I'd deliberately stage the actual work -- batch by batch, with an export taken before each batch -- specifically so that if someone pushes back partway through, I'm not stuck having already merged everything irreversibly. If a department does push back mid-project, my first move is to pause that department's remaining batches, not defend the work already done -- I'd go look at the specific records they're concerned about, and if there's a real issue (a matching rule being too aggressive for their specific data patterns), I'd fix the matching criteria before resuming, rather than assuming my original dedup logic was correct and trying to convince them to accept it.
commonMistakes: Running the merge as a single irreversible action instead of staged, exportable batches
Not communicating specifics (counts, what a merge changes) before starting, only a vague notice
Defending completed work instead of pausing and investigating when a department pushes back
Not giving departments a real chance to flag false-positive matches before merging
keyPoints: Communicate specifics (affected record counts, what merge actually changes) before starting, not a vague notice
Give departments a real window to flag records before merging
Run the project in staged, exportable/reversible batches rather than one irreversible action
Pause and investigate when pushback occurs rather than defending completed work

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes specific, upfront communication rather than a vague notice
Describes a staged, reversible approach rather than one big irreversible action
Responds to mid-project pushback by pausing and investigating
Gives departments a real chance to flag issues before merging

questions.title: Two Departments Want Conflicting Things From the Same Report
questions.prompt: Sales wants a shared pipeline report to show only open Opportunities so it looks cleaner for their weekly review, while Finance wants the same report to include Closed Won and Closed Lost for forecasting accuracy. Both think their version is the right one. How do you resolve it?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer recognizes this isn't actually a single-report conflict to referee -- it's two genuinely different reporting needs that happen to be aimed at the same underlying report object, and the right resolution is usually to build two separate reports (or a base report plus a saved filtered view) serving each audience correctly, rather than picking one department's preference and making the other unhappy, or trying to force one report with a compromise filter that serves neither need well. The answer should describe going back to both stakeholders with that reframing -- explaining that maintaining one shared report everyone has to compromise on isn't actually necessary, and that each team can get exactly what they need without taking anything away from the other, which usually resolves the 'conflict' because it was never really about the two sides disagreeing on facts, just about assuming the report had to be singular.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first move is pointing out that this doesn't actually have to be a fight over one report -- Sales needing an open-pipeline view and Finance needing a full forecasting view are both completely legitimate, they're just different questions being asked of the same data, which doesn't require a single shared answer. I'd propose building a Sales-specific report filtered to open Opportunities for their weekly review, and a separate Finance-specific report including all stages for forecasting, both pulling from the same underlying Opportunity data so there's no risk of the two reports disagreeing on the facts, just differing on scope. I'd bring that reframing back to both groups rather than trying to broker a single compromise filter, because a 50/50 compromise (like a time-boxed or partially filtered version) usually ends up genuinely wrong for both uses rather than acceptable for either -- Sales still sees clutter, and Finance still doesn't get full accuracy.
commonMistakes: Trying to resolve this with a single compromise report that serves neither need well
Picking one department's version and treating the other's concern as less important
Not recognizing this as 'two different reports needed,' not a factual disagreement to settle
Not ensuring both reports pull from the same underlying data to avoid future inconsistency
keyPoints: Recognize this as two legitimate, different needs, not a single report to compromise on
Propose two separate, audience-specific reports rather than one filtered compromise
Both reports should pull from the same underlying data for consistency
Reframe the conversation with both stakeholders rather than picking a side

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Recognizes this isn't a factual disagreement needing a single answer
Proposes two separate audience-specific reports as the resolution
Ensures consistency by pulling from the same underlying data
Communicates the reframing back to both stakeholders

questions.title: Explaining a Schema Change Tradeoff to a Business Stakeholder
questions.prompt: You've determined that a requested change -- making 'Site Visit' a child of 'Property' via master-detail instead of lookup, to enable a roll-up count the business wants -- means Site Visits will be permanently deleted if a Property is ever deleted. The business stakeholder just wants the roll-up and doesn't think about the rest. How do you explain this?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer doesn't just implement the requested feature (the roll-up) and silently accept the side effect, nor does it refuse the request outright -- it explains the actual tradeoff in terms the stakeholder can evaluate, specifically: 'to get the automatic visit-count number you want, this change also means that if a Property record is ever deleted, every Site Visit tied to it gets deleted too, with no separate undo for those -- is that acceptable, or is there a reason Properties might get deleted that would make this risky?' This surfaces the real question (is Property deletion actually likely or governed) rather than assuming the answer, and offers the honest alternative (a non-cascading roll-up built another way, slightly more setup, no cascading-delete risk) so the stakeholder is making an informed choice rather than discovering the side effect later when a Property gets deleted by accident.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't just build the master-detail relationship because it's the 'free' way to get a roll-up, and I also wouldn't refuse to give them the roll-up at all -- I'd go back and explain specifically what they're trading for that convenience: 'I can set this up so Property automatically shows a running count of its Site Visits, but doing it the simplest way also means deleting a Property would delete all its Site Visits permanently, with no separate recovery for just the visits. Is that an acceptable risk given how Properties get deleted in practice, or should I build the count a different way that avoids that risk but takes a bit more setup?' That question usually surfaces something I wouldn't have known -- maybe Properties are never actually hard-deleted in this org, which makes the risk basically theoretical, or maybe they are deleted occasionally for data cleanup, which tells me the safer, non-cascading approach is actually worth the extra setup. Either way, the stakeholder ends up making an informed decision instead of me quietly picking for them and them finding out about the side effect the hard way.
commonMistakes: Implementing the simplest technical solution without surfacing the real tradeoff to the stakeholder
Refusing to deliver the requested roll-up instead of explaining the tradeoff and offering an alternative
Not asking about actual Property deletion practices to gauge whether the risk is real or theoretical
Explaining the tradeoff in technical terms (master-detail, cascading delete) without plain-language consequences
keyPoints: Surface the real tradeoff in plain terms before implementing, not after
Ask about actual deletion practices to judge whether the risk is theoretical or real
Offer the safer alternative (non-cascading roll-up) so the stakeholder can make an informed choice
Avoid both silently implementing the risky option and flatly refusing the request

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Surfaces the real tradeoff clearly before implementing
Asks a concrete question to assess real-world risk (deletion practices)
Offers a genuine alternative rather than a flat refusal
Explains the consequence in plain, non-jargon terms

questions.title: An Urgent Access Request Comes in Outside the Normal Process
questions.prompt: A VP emails you directly asking you to grant a contractor full access to a sensitive object right now, bypassing the normal change-request and approval process, because 'it's urgent and we don't have time for the usual steps.' How do you respond?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer doesn't rigidly refuse ('I can't do anything without the full process') or simply comply because a VP asked -- it separates the two real concerns: the request may well be genuinely urgent and legitimate, and that urgency can usually be honored quickly without skipping the parts of the process that actually matter for security (knowing exactly what's being granted and to whom, and having it documented). The right move is to ask what's actually needed right now versus what can follow slightly after -- often granting a narrowly scoped permission set immediately (which takes minutes) while still logging the request and getting it documented/approved just after the fact rather than before, satisfies the real urgency without fully bypassing accountability; a flat refusal in the name of process isn't actually serving the business either, so the goal is finding the fast path that still leaves a record and keeps scope narrow, not skipping the process entirely.
questions.professionalAnswer: My response wouldn't be an immediate yes or an immediate no -- I'd say something like, 'I can get this contractor access within the next few minutes, but I want to scope it to exactly what they need right now rather than full access to the object, and I'll log this as an expedited request today so there's a record, rather than skipping documentation altogether.' That addresses the actual time pressure (minutes, not days) without doing the one thing that actually worries me about 'just skip the process' -- having no record of who got what access and why, which is exactly the kind of gap that causes real problems later when nobody remembers why a contractor had broad access to sensitive data. If the VP pushes back and insists on literally full, unscoped access right now with zero documentation, I'd hold that specific line and explain why -- not to be difficult, but because that specific combination (broad scope, zero record) is the actual risk, not the speed.
commonMistakes: Refusing entirely in the name of process, ignoring genuine urgency
Granting full, unscoped access immediately just because a VP asked
Skipping documentation/logging entirely to save time
Not distinguishing which parts of the process are actually safety-critical versus just procedural
keyPoints: Separate genuine urgency from the request to skip accountability entirely
Offer a fast path: scoped access granted quickly, documented just after rather than skipped
Hold the line specifically on scope and documentation, not on speed
A VP's request doesn't override the need for a record of who was granted what access and why

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Avoids both rigid refusal and unquestioning compliance
Proposes a concrete fast path that still preserves scope and documentation
Identifies documentation/record-keeping as the actual safety-critical element
Shows willingness to hold a line on the right specific issue, not on speed itself

questions.title: A stakeholder wants a new field added mid-sprint
questions.prompt: Your team is three days into a two-week sprint when a stakeholder asks you to add a new field to a report you're already building, saying it's 'quick, shouldn't change anything.' Walk me through how you'd actually handle this request.
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer doesn't just say yes or no -- it describes a specific process for evaluating a mid-sprint request honestly before committing to it. First, actually assess the request rather than taking 'quick' at face value: does the new field require touching the dataset's underlying query, does it interact with existing filters or parameters, does it need its own testing? Second, be transparent with the stakeholder and the team about the real tradeoff: if it genuinely is small, say so and fold it in; if it's not, explain specifically why (not vaguely) and present the actual options -- add it now and risk the sprint's committed work, or add it to the next sprint, or (if it's urgent) swap it in for something already committed and explicitly deprioritized. The point to get across is that this isn't about being rigid or unhelpful -- it's about making the tradeoff visible instead of silently absorbing scope and then explaining later why other committed work slipped.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't just say yes because it's described as quick, and I also wouldn't flatly refuse because 'that's not what we committed to' -- I'd actually go look at what the change requires first. If it really is a one-column addition to an existing dataset with no filter interactions, I'd just do it and move on, because treating every tiny request as a formal change-control event is its own kind of overhead. But if it touches the dataset's query, interacts with parameters already in play, or needs real testing, I'd say that specifically and honestly, rather than agreeing and then quietly having something else slip. I'd lay out the actual choice for the stakeholder and my Product Owner: we can add this now and something else committed to this sprint moves to next sprint, or this goes into the next sprint's backlog, or if it's genuinely urgent, I'll tell you specifically what I'd need to drop to make room for it. What I'm protecting isn't my own workload -- it's the team's ability to make an honest commitment and actually hit it, instead of everyone quietly absorbing 'just one more small thing' until the sprint's real scope bears no resemblance to what was planned.
commonMistakes: Automatically agreeing to the request without actually assessing its real scope first
Refusing rigidly without explaining the real tradeoff or offering alternatives
Silently absorbing the extra work and letting already-committed work slip without telling anyone why
Not involving the Product Owner or team in the actual tradeoff decision
keyPoints: Actually assesses the request's real scope instead of taking 'quick' at face value
Is transparent about the tradeoff rather than silently absorbing scope creep
Presents concrete options (do it now and drop something, defer it, or swap priorities)
Frames the goal as protecting the team's ability to make honest commitments, not personal workload

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes actually assessing the request's real scope rather than assuming
Shows transparent communication about the tradeoff involved
Presents concrete, realistic options rather than a flat yes/no
Frames this as protecting the team's commitments, not personal convenience

questions.title: Communicating a blocker in the daily standup
questions.prompt: You're stuck on a task -- a stored procedure change you need is waiting on another team's approval -- and it's been blocked for two days. How would you bring this up in the daily standup, and what would you do about it outside of standup?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer treats the Daily Scrum correctly -- as a short team sync, not a status report to a manager -- and keeps the standup update itself brief and specific: what's blocked, who or what it's waiting on, and how long it's been stuck, rather than a long explanation of the underlying technical problem. The real work happens outside standup: actually escalating the blocker rather than just mentioning it and waiting -- following up directly with whoever owns the approval, looping in the Scrum Master if the blocker is specifically the kind of cross-team obstacle they're meant to help clear, and being honest with the team about the sprint-goal impact if it stays stuck much longer, rather than quietly hoping it resolves itself. The key distinction a strong answer draws is between mentioning a blocker (passive) and actively working to clear it (what's actually expected).
questions.professionalAnswer: In standup itself, I'd keep it tight: 'I'm blocked on the stored procedure change -- it's been waiting on sign-off from the other team for two days now, and I don't have a resolution plan yet.' That's it -- standup isn't the place to walk through the technical details or vent about how annoying the wait is; it's a quick sync so the team knows where things stand. The actual work happens right after standup, not during it. I'd go directly to whoever on the other team owns that approval and ask specifically what's holding it up and when I can expect it, rather than just waiting passively for two more days. If that doesn't move things, I'd loop in my Scrum Master specifically, because clearing exactly this kind of cross-team blocker is their job, not something I should be expected to just push through alone. And if it looks like this is going to threaten the sprint goal, I'd say that out loud to the team well before the sprint review, not as a surprise at the end -- being blocked isn't a failure on my part, but sitting on it quietly without escalating would be.
commonMistakes: Treating the standup as the place to explain the full technical backstory instead of a brief status
Mentioning the blocker in standup but then passively waiting instead of actively escalating it afterward
Not involving the Scrum Master, whose job specifically includes clearing cross-team blockers
Waiting until the sprint review to surface that the blocker threatened the sprint goal
keyPoints: The Daily Scrum update should be brief and specific, not a technical deep dive
Mentioning a blocker in standup isn't the same as actively working to clear it
Escalating directly to the other team and/or the Scrum Master is the appropriate next step
Sprint-goal risk should be surfaced early, not held until the sprint review

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes an appropriately brief, specific standup update
Describes actively escalating the blocker outside of standup, not just waiting
Correctly involves the Scrum Master's actual role in clearing blockers
Shows early, honest communication about sprint-goal risk

questions.title: Two stakeholders both want their ticket done first
questions.prompt: You have two open tickets: a bug fix a sales manager is pushing for urgently, and a new report feature your own manager assigned last week with a deadline that's actually sooner. Both stakeholders think their request is the priority. How do you handle it?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer doesn't unilaterally decide between two stakeholders' competing priorities on its own authority -- it recognizes that prioritization decisions belong with whoever actually owns the backlog's priority order (a Product Owner, in Scrum terms, or whoever plays that role on the team), and surfaces the conflict to them explicitly rather than quietly picking one and hoping the other doesn't notice. The practical first step is gathering the actual facts needed to make the decision -- how urgent is the bug really (is it actively breaking something for users right now, or just annoying), and what's the real deadline and consequence of missing it for the report feature -- rather than just taking either stakeholder's framing of urgency at face value. Then bring both pieces of information to whoever should decide, make the conflict and the tradeoff explicit, and get an actual decision rather than silently deprioritizing one person's request without them knowing.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't try to quietly referee this myself between two people who each think their thing is most important -- that's not actually my call to make alone, and if I just pick one, I've effectively made a business priority decision without the authority or the full context to make it well. My first step is getting the real facts: is this bug actually breaking something in production right now, or is it an annoyance that feels urgent but isn't actually blocking anyone? What's the real, hard deadline on the report feature, and what actually happens if it slips a few days? Once I have real answers instead of just each stakeholder's own sense of urgency, I'd go to whoever actually owns prioritization for my work -- my manager, or a Product Owner if that's how the team is structured -- lay out both asks and their actual urgency side by side, and ask for an explicit call. I'd rather spend ten minutes getting a clear decision than spend a day guessing which stakeholder to disappoint and then having to explain that choice after the fact.
commonMistakes: Unilaterally deciding between two stakeholders' competing priorities without the authority or full context to do so
Taking either stakeholder's self-reported urgency at face value instead of verifying the actual impact and deadline
Quietly deprioritizing one request without telling that stakeholder, letting them find out later
Not escalating to whoever actually owns prioritization decisions for the team's work
keyPoints: Prioritization conflicts between stakeholders should be escalated, not unilaterally resolved
Gathers real facts about urgency and deadlines rather than accepting either framing at face value
Brings both pieces of information to whoever owns the priority decision for an explicit call
Avoids silently deprioritizing a stakeholder without their knowledge

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Recognizes this isn't a unilateral decision and escalates appropriately
Describes gathering real facts about urgency/impact before escalating
Describes a clear, explicit escalation with both pieces of information presented
Avoids silently disappointing either stakeholder without communication

questions.title: A ticket has no acceptance criteria
questions.prompt: You pick up a ticket from the sprint backlog that says 'Add a filter for region to the sales dashboard' with no further detail -- no acceptance criteria, no mention of default behavior or how it should interact with existing filters. What do you do before writing any code?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer resists the temptation to just start building based on a guess, because a story without acceptance criteria is genuinely too vague to know when it's actually done -- 'I think this is done' and a shared, checkable definition of done are different things, and building against the wrong assumption wastes real time for both the developer and whoever has to send it back. The right move is going back to whoever owns the ticket -- the Product Owner or the stakeholder who requested it -- and asking specific, concrete questions rather than one vague 'what do you mean': what should the filter's default value be, does it need to interact with (cascade from or into) any existing filters already on the dashboard, and is there a specific list of regions or should it reflect whatever's in the data. Writing those answers down as explicit acceptance criteria before starting, not after, turns a vague request into something both the developer and whoever reviews the finished work can actually check against.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't start building off a guess, because 'add a filter for region' sounds simple but actually hides several real decisions -- what region data source is sensible as the dropdown's default, whether this filter needs to interact with any filter already on the dashboard, whether 'region' even means the same thing across every table the dashboard touches. Guessing wrong on any of those means I build something, it gets reviewed, and it comes back with changes -- which is slower overall than just asking upfront. So before writing anything, I'd go back to whoever owns the ticket with specific questions, not a vague 'can you clarify this' -- I'd ask directly: should this default to the viewer's own region if we track that, does selecting a region need to affect any other filter already on the page, and is there an existing region list I should match or is this open-ended. Once I have real answers, I'd write them down as the ticket's acceptance criteria myself if nobody else does, specifically so there's a shared, checkable definition everyone agrees to before I start -- that protects me too, since I now have something concrete to point back to if the request changes later.
commonMistakes: Starting to build based on a guess instead of clarifying ambiguous requirements first
Asking a vague 'can you clarify this ticket' instead of specific, concrete questions
Not writing down the clarified requirements as explicit acceptance criteria before starting
Assuming the ticket's brevity means the request is actually simple, missing the real decisions hidden inside it
keyPoints: A story without acceptance criteria is genuinely too vague to know when it's actually done
Asks specific, concrete clarifying questions rather than a vague request for more detail
Writes down the clarified requirements as explicit acceptance criteria before starting work
Clarifying upfront is faster overall than building on a guess and having it sent back

questions.title: The Business Says the Dashboard You Built Isn't What They Asked For
questions.prompt: You finish a dashboard, it passes your own testing, and then the business stakeholder reviews it in UAT and says it doesn't actually answer what they needed. How do you respond, and how do you prevent the same gap next time?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer treats a UAT rejection as a normal, expected signal rather than a personal failure or a sign the stakeholder is being difficult — UAT exists specifically to catch the case where code is technically correct but isn't actually what the business needed, which is a different question than QA's "does it work correctly" entirely. The right immediate response is to ask specific, concrete questions rather than getting defensive: what exactly does the current version show, what were they expecting instead, and can they point to a specific number or view that's wrong relative to their mental model. Often the real gap traces back to acceptance criteria that were vague or incomplete at the start, not a build mistake — which is the actual thing to fix going forward: writing more specific, checkable acceptance criteria during intake (edge cases included, like what a zero-sales region should display) so UAT becomes a confirmation step rather than where requirements gaps first surface.
questions.professionalAnswer: First thing I'd do is not get defensive about it, because UAT rejecting something isn't the same as me having done something wrong — it's literally what that stage is for, catching the gap between 'this is technically correct' and 'this is actually what we needed,' which are genuinely different questions. I'd ask specific questions rather than just apologizing and reworking blindly: what exactly were you expecting to see here, can you show me a specific number that looks wrong to you versus what you expected. Usually when I dig into it, the real root cause isn't that I built the wrong thing technically — it's that the original request or acceptance criteria were vague enough that I made a reasonable assumption that just wasn't the assumption they were making. Going forward, the actual fix isn't 'be more careful next time,' it's writing tighter, more specific acceptance criteria up front — including the edge cases, like what happens when a region has zero sales for the month — so that gap gets caught during planning instead of surfacing for the first time in UAT.
commonMistakes: Treating a UAT rejection as a personal failure or getting defensive instead of investigating specifically
Reworking the dashboard based on a vague complaint without asking specific clarifying questions first
Not tracing the root cause back to incomplete acceptance criteria, repeating the same gap on the next project
Assuming the stakeholder is simply wrong instead of taking their feedback as a genuine signal about the request
keyPoints: UAT exists specifically to catch 'technically correct but not what was needed,' a different question than QA
The right response is specific clarifying questions, not defensiveness or blind rework
The root cause is often vague acceptance criteria at intake, not a build mistake
The real fix is tighter acceptance criteria going forward, including edge cases

questions.title: A Dashboard Goes Live, and Immediately Something's Wrong
questions.prompt: Two days after a new regional revenue dashboard launches, a regional manager reports it's showing zero sales for their region, which is obviously wrong. Walk through how you'd investigate this and what you'd communicate to the regional manager while you're still figuring it out.
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer separates the investigation from the communication, and gets both moving in parallel rather than going silent until the fix is found. On investigation, the logical order is checking the environments closest to the symptom first: is this specific region's data actually present in the underlying source as of the relevant date, did the scheduled refresh for this model actually complete successfully (checking refresh history for errors), and does any report-level filter (RLS, a regional filter default) unintentionally exclude this region's rows. On communication, the mistake to avoid is going quiet until the root cause is fully found — the right move is an immediate, honest acknowledgment that specifically names what's being checked ("I've confirmed the issue and I'm checking whether it's a refresh failure or a filter problem, I'll update you within the hour") rather than either a vague "looking into it" or disappearing until there's a complete answer, since a specific update lets the regional manager decide what to do in the meantime (for example, whether to trust other numbers from the same report).
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd do two things essentially at the same time: start investigating, and send the regional manager something specific right away rather than going quiet until I have a full answer. On the investigation side, I'd work from the symptom outward — first checking refresh history to see whether last night's scheduled refresh for this model actually succeeded, since a failed or partial refresh is a really common cause of 'this one region looks wrong.' If the refresh is fine, I'd check whether the region's data is actually present in the source table for the relevant date, and then check whether any filter — RLS, a default slicer, anything report-level — is quietly excluding that region specifically. On the communication side, I'd send something concrete almost immediately, like 'I've confirmed something's wrong with the regional number, I'm checking whether it's a refresh issue or a filter issue right now, I'll have an update for you within the hour' — specific enough that they know I've actually looked at it and know roughly when to expect more, rather than a vague 'we're on it' that tells them nothing.
commonMistakes: Going silent until the root cause is fully found instead of sending a specific interim update
Guessing at the cause instead of checking refresh history and filters methodically
Sending a vague 'we're looking into it' instead of naming what's specifically being checked
Fixing the symptom without identifying why it happened, risking a repeat next refresh cycle
keyPoints: Investigation and communication should happen in parallel, not sequentially
A methodical check order: refresh history, source data presence, then report-level filters
A specific interim update is far more useful than a vague one or silence
The regional manager should know roughly when to expect a further update

Describes a specific, honest interim communication, not silence or vagueness
Recognizes investigation and communication should happen together
Mentions follow-up to prevent recurrence
